speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) the House went into Committee to considerable following proposed resolution, Mr. Blain in the Chair:
Resolved,-That it is expedient
1.	To repeal subsection two of section twenty-six of the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908, and provide that any person placed in the Third Division upon the coming into force of that Act, and who had theretofore passed the Qualifying Examination, may be promoted from the Third Division to the Second Division by the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the head of the Department based upon the report in writing of the deputy head.
2.	That sections twenty-nine and thirty and subsection one of section thirty-two of the said Act be repealed and that it be provided that in the Second Division the minimum and maximum salaries shall he as follows:-
In subdivision A, $1,600 to $2,100 ;
In subdivision B, $1,000 to $1,600 ; that in the Third Division the minimum and maximum salaries shall he as follows:-
In subdivision B, $500 to $1,000;
In subdivision A, $1,000 to $1,300 ; and that the minimum and maximum salaries for the positions of messenger, porter, sorter and packer and such other positions in the lower grades as are determined by the Governor in Council shall be $500 and $1,000 respectively.
3.	That it he provided that the Governor In Council may grant an increase of one hundred dollars to any clerk in the Third Division of the Inside Service of the Civil Service and to any person holding any of the positions mentioned in section thirty-two of the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908, who
(a)	is reported by the deputy head to be deserving of such increase; and
(b)	is in receipt of a salary of less than one thousand dollars.
4.	That it he provided that any person now serving in either the Second or Third Division of the Inside Service whose salary is less than the minimum salary for such division as proposed by the second of the preceding Resolutions shall have his salary increased to such minimum.
5.	That it be provided that all increases granted under legislation to he based upon the third and fourth of the preceding Resolutions shall take effect from the first day of April, one thousand nine hundred and seventeen.
6.	That it be provided that nothing in the legislation to be based upon these Resolutions shall prevent any person from receiving any annual or other increase that may he granted to him under any other Act.
7.	That it be provided that any payments or increases authorized by any legislation based upon these resolutions he payable out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
Owing to the
conditions which have prevailed for some

time past, and which have been accentuated during the last few months of the war, it has been considered expedient to bring down legislation to provide for the increases and other changes set forth in this resolution. When I placed the resolution upon the Order Paper, I was under the impression that under section 33 of the Civil Service Act it* would be open to the Government to grant a minimum salary of more than $500. I find that that is not quite a correct understanding of the position, and I therefore have to suggest an amendment to provide that the minimum salary in subdivision A of the Third Division be $600 instead of $500. This minimum salary of $600 will also apply to the messenger, porter, sorter and packer class referred to in one of the provisions of the Civil Service Act, I have a further amendment to propose with regard to those in the Second Division, to the effect that the annual increase be $100 instead of $50 as at present provided. Substantially what is proposed is this: In the Third Division, the salaries in subdivision A, which are now from $900 to $1,200, will be from $1,000 to $1,300; and in subdivision B, where the salaries now .are from $500 to $800, they will be from $600 to $1,000. We further provide, with respect to the messengers, porters, sorters, packers, and certain other positions in the lower grades determined by the Governor General in Council under the Civil Service Act, that the minimum and maximum shall be $600 and $1,000 respectively. It is further provided, in order tr meet conditions as to the higher cost of living, that the Government may grant an increase of $100 to any clerk in the Third Division of the Inside Service, or to any person holding any otheT position mentioned in Section 32 of the Civil Service Amendment Act of 1908,- that is, messenger, sorter, or packer-who is reported 'by the deputy head to be deserving of such increase, and who has now a salary of less than $1,000.
The legislation will also provide that any person now serving in the Third Division of the Inside Service, whose salary is less than the minimum salary for such division, as proposed by these resolutions, shall have his salary increased to such minimum. That is, if a clerk is getting $500 he goes to $600, as that is the minimum which we provide. We propose further that the increases granted under this legislation shall take effect from April 1 last-that is they shall begin with the present fiscal year.
In order to meet what has been regarded by the Service and the Government as a grievance on the part of certain of the Service in the Third Division, who had passed the qualifying examination prior to the enactment of the present Civil Service Act, we provide that they may be promoted from the Third Division to the Second Division, upon the report in writing of the deputy head. I shall, if required, explain that more in detail when the section concerning it is under consideration by the committee. In order to provide for the amendments I have- indicated, I- beg to lay upon the Table the resolution in full, with the changes which I have suggested-namely,, the minimum salary raised from $500 to $600 in respect to those I have named; and' an increase of $100 per annum instead of" $50 -per annum in the Second Division.
'Mr. MURPHY:	Would the minister be
kind enough to explain the application of subsection 6 of the resolution?

iMr. DEVLIN: Will the minister be good enough to tell the House what the letter carriers will get by this resolution?

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
This applies to
the Inside Service. I understand that the case of the letter carriers is under consideration 'by the Postmaster General. I stated some time ago that in so far as the Inside Service is concerned, we should deal with it by legislation and that in so far as the Outside Service is concerned, the matter would be dealt with in the Supplementary Estimates. Provision will have to be made in the Supplementary Estimates to the ex-

tent of the amount necessary to take care of the recommendations of the ministers with respect to the Outside Service.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Will the labouring classes, the carpenters, electricians and others receive absolutely nothing under this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
This resolution
's an amendment to the present Civil Service Act. Being an amending Act, it does not cover more than is covered by the present Civil Service Act. The case of those in the Outside Sewice as distinguished from the Inside Service will be dealt aa it is now dealt with under existing legislation in the Estimates and upon the recommendation of the minister. Take, for example, a customs official; the Minister of Custom's may bring before the Treasury Board, and through the Treasury Board to Council, a recommendation that $50 or ?100 be added to the salary of that , customs official. The money to pay for that increase is provided for in the Estimates. The Outside Service is always dealt with on the recommendation of the ministers through the Treasury Board 'by Council and by Parliament toy. assenting to the votes, which are contained each year in the Estimates.
' Mr. DEVLIN:	Does not the minister
think that the better way to meet the increased cost of living would be by giving the Service all round a bonus of $100 and by raising the yearly increases from $50 to $100?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
There are many considerations arising in connection with this question. In the first place, there is a desire on the part of all of us to do justice to the Civil Service. On the other hand, we cannot lose sight of the public. The salaries of the civil servants run from $500 to $5,000. When we get up to salaries ranging from $2,000 to $3,000 and $4,000, they are fairly substantial as compared with salaries outside. It is in connection with the lower grades of the Service that the pinch comes. I think we must have regard to public bpiiinionj I should doubt as to whether public opinion would be favourable to a wholesale increase in the salaries of civil servants. We have thought that we have reasonably met the situation-and I believe the Civil 'Service feel that we have done so-in dealing with the Third Division and with the Second Division by increasing the minimum and the maximum in the
fSir Thomas White.!
Third Division, by providing for annual increases of $100 instead of $50 in the Second Division and by dealing with messengers, sorters and packers in the way 1 have indicated. Having given the whole matter a great deal of consideration and having been in consultation with the representatives of the Civil Service, unless I am entirely misinformed, I think I am safe in saying that this Bill will substantially meet the situation as far as the Inside Service is concerned with which it purposes to deal. This does not mean that the Outside Service will not be dealt with. We are introducing legislation for the purpose of amending the. existing Civil Service Act which applies only to the Inside Service and which is necessary to meet present conditions.

speechtext: There is only one more point and I shall have finished. I have received several communications in connection with this .resolution and a good many along this line. Here is a man who writes to me and says that he was appointed in 1902, that he passed the qualifying examination in 1904, that in 1906 he was appointed to the junior second class, and that in the spring of 1908 he passed the promotion examination. In the spring of 1908 he had all the papers necessary for his appointment to the senior second class settled, but owing to a delay caused by the Treasury Board they were left on the shelf too long. The result was that on September 1, 1908, the Civil Service Act was passed and his papers were of no value. He was classed, a3 he then was, as a junior second class clerk and went automatically into class A of the third division. He was then getting $1,150. He got the $150 increase that was given to all the service at that time, but that only benefited him by the s.um of $50, as that put him to the maximum of $1,200. He represents that he has lost $2,000 since.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: You mean that he cannot take the examination that would take him out?

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: No. This particular man whose letter I read is in charge of a branch. He has a secretary and four clerks working under him and the clerks are receiving a higher salary than he gets. Others in the same department who have been working there 20 years are getting $1,200. I understand there are some such in the Post Office Department, others in the Interior Department, and others, again, in other departments. Will this resolution benefit that class in any rvay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: If my hon. friend will observe "the first section of the resolution he will see that we propose to provide that any person placed in the third division upon the coming into force of the Civil Service Act, and who theretofore had passed the qualifying examination, may be promoted from the third to the second division by the Governor General in Council upon the recommendation of the head of the department, 'based upon a request in writing from the deputy head.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: At what salary would he go in? At the minimum, he gets $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
No. The point is this: when the Civil Service Act was passed in 1908 there were men in the Civil Service who had passed the qualifying examination and some the promotion examination. I believe I am within the mark in stating that the Government of the day did not intend that these men should be obliged to pass an academic examination to 'qualify them for higher positions. Nevertheless, on account of the attitude taken towards the legislation by the Civil Service Commission, men in that class have found themselves obliged either to take the [DOT]academic examination or to remain in that class, no matter what their office qualifications might be.
Now there are many men who have passed the age at which they could get up the work necessary to pass a stiff academic examination, quite the equivalent of university matriculation. I doubt very much if there is a man in this House who to-day could pass the matriculation examination, or even the entrance examination to the high school. I do not believe there is a man here who could pass the matriculation.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: I would not emphasize that too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: I doubt if even the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) could pass the matriculation examination. I do not mean to say that if he applied his intelligence, great as we know it to be, to study for say six months or a year he would not be able to get through- barely get through.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that the hqn. member for St. John would persuade the examiners -that he had passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
Yes, I think if he tried to pass he would manage in some way to pass. At all events, it has seemed to us that this constitutes a real hardship. I am not blaming the Civil Service Commission. I am not passing any censure on them. No doubt they are discharging their duty as they see it, but it does seem to me that it is a real hardship that those men who had been in the service prior to the passing of the legislation should be forced to pass an academic examination to get out of that class, notwithstanding that they might be exceedingly competent in the duties of their office. Without elaborating too much on that, I may say that I have looked up the matter and I find *that in all Civil Service legislation passed prior to that date, the rights of those in the service were observed; and, further than that, I may say that, so far as I can gather from the debates, it was not the intention of the late Government that these men should be compelled to pass an academic examination in order to get out of that class. In proof of that I propos'e to read to the House one or two extracts from Hansard. For example, the Hon. Mr. Fisher, who I believe had charge of the Bill, said in the debates of the session of 1908, on page 11378:
The Civil Service is to-day established on certain lines; the men who have entered the Civil Service have entered it on certain conditions and are entitled to the consideration due to those who are in the place which they have attained to under certain laws, rules and regulations. We are proposing a new and more difficult entrance to the Civil Service, but we have to recognize the rights of those who are to-day in the service.
And then in the Senate Sir Mackenzie Bowell, at page 1600 of the debates of 1908, referring to the third class clerks, asked:
Will that officer be compelled to go before the new Commission and be examined again before he can be promoted?
The Hon. Mr. Scott, representing the Government in the Senate, replied:
I think not. It would not be fair. I do not think the Bill is intended to be ex post facto ; it is intended to be prospective. The Act will not go into force until September, because it will take some time to organize under it. It is quite impossible to fathom exactly where it will lead to, but I think I am quite safe in saying that an official who is now qualified for promotion could not be disturbed.
Then, Mr. Fisher, in dealing with the provision of the Civil Service Act which provided that men of this class might be eligible for promotion with or without examination, said:
With or without examination, as is determined by the regulations of the commission.
Then he goes on to say:
The principle adopted is to leave to the Commission the way in which they would obtain their information on which to base their certi-

ficate of qualification. They may do that on the record of the clerks in the department without making any examination, and they might on it give a certificate of qualification for a promotion. Or they might not think that conclusive, and they might prefer to hold an examination. They might also think it better to hold a competitive examination. They would not hold a competitive examination unless the head of the department nominated two or three different clerks in it for promotion.
It is perfectly clear to me that when the Civil Service Act was brought down, following the practice that had been adopted in previous legislation of the sort, it was the intention of the Government that those who were in the third class in the -Service should be eligible for promotion without having to pass a stiff examination, that is to say, if they had passed the qualifying examination. There has undoubtedly been a great deal of feeling in the Civil Service that there has been an injustice to that class. I think there is substantial ground for that feeling. I do not pass any adverse criticism upon the Civil Service Commission. They, no doubt, as I have said, are carrying out their duties as they think they	ought, but	the fact remainsthat under	that Civil	Service Act
a number of very capable men have been denied promotion because they have not been able to take the academic examination. I have taken the trouble to* make inquiry among deputies on whose judgment I feel I can rely, and they tell me there are many cases indeed of hardship in which men such as the man referred to by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, well qualified men, c-annot get out of that class because they cannot take a stiff academic examination.

speechtext: I am speaking of the third division; I will speak later of the class referred to by my hon. friend. speechtext: Are the civil servants who are serving at the front receiving the statutory increases the same as those who remain at home? I am told that they are not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
I am speaking
again from recollection, but with some positiveness. I believe that this is the situation. At first, when a civil servant enlisted, it was provided that he should receive the salary which he was getting in the Civil Service. I think the annual increase was overlooked. My recollection, and my advice from my colleague here (Mr. ' Crothers), is that an Order in Council was passed to provide for the statutory increases being given.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
To those at the
front ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: To those at the front, so that they will find themselves when they come-back in the same position as they would have been if they had not enlisted. If that has not been done, I can say it will be done, but I think it has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
If it has not
been done, it will be done.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
I am informed that a
third Order in Council dealing with civil servants has recently been passed, under which a civil servant if he enlists receives no portion of his salary. Is that the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: I think an Order in Council of that nature has been passed, but that was in view of the. compulsory service legislation which is about to be brought down.	.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: That is not passed yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: At all events that point does not seem to be relevant to this matter.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: It is peculiar that the Government should pass an Order in Council in view of legislation that has not yet been considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
In regard to enlistments from the Civil Service, I have been informed by Civil Service representatives that the total enlistments
4 p.m. from the Civil Service at Ottawa are 981, and that the total enlistments from the Civil Service outside of Ottawa are 2,^27, making a total enlistment from the whole service of 3,808. That is stated to be an incomplete return, as no records of new enlistments have been received from several departments for some weeks past, and there is one department in which there is no complete record. This legislation applies to all who are at present in the Civil Service. If the compulsory service legislation is passed, as I believe it will be, then the Civil Service will be subject to its provisions just the same as individuals outside of the Civil Service. The Civil Service, it seems to me, is in the same position to-day as the rest of the community; that is to say, there has not been compulsory service enforced by the Government; the enlistment so far has been voluntary; it has been open to a member of the Civil Service, as it has been open to any one outside, to volunteer or not to volunteer, and this resolution which I have brought in applies to the Civil Service as it stands to-day, those who have enlisted and those who have not enlisted,

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
It is a most extraordinary thing for the Government to pass an Order in Council discriminating, from the date of the passing of the Order, which I understand was about a week ago, against civil servants who may enlist, irrespective altogether of the coming into force of any compulsory service. I have seen it stated in the papers, and I am told it is true that an Order in Council has been passed providing that those members of the Civil Service who enlist after the passing of the Order shall not be entitled to receive any portion of their salary. That Order, in Council has been passed altogether irrespective of compulsory service, and indeed I think it is an extraordinary assumption for the Government to pass an Order in Council

the effect of which is to discourage civil servants from voluntary enlistment, and to state that that Order is passed in view of a compulsory measure which may or may not be passed. If I were a member of the Government I would not like to assume what the House of Commons or the Senate might do; I would rather wait until the measure was explained to Parliament and until Parliament had taken action with reference to it. The effect of this Order in Council is to say to every civil servant: If you enlist after this Order is passed you will be discriminated against; you will be treated in a different way from that in which other civil servants have been treated. It is in effect the Government saying to every civil servant: We do not want you to enlist. If my information is correct we have three distinct and contradictory provisions in regard to the Civil Service. We have one class of enlisted civil servants, who receive not only their military pay, but their full Civil Service pay; we have another class of enlisted civil servants who receive their military pay and the difference between their Civil Service pay and their military pay, and now, under this last Order in Council, we have another class of enlisted civil servants who will receive simply their military pay, and who have been deprived altogether of their Civil Service pay. It seems to me that is an extraordinary state of affairs to have three different provisions relating to the same class of boys who may enlist for service at the front.	-
While I am on my feet let me ask the minister why he makes this provision in paragraph " 3 " of the resolution:-
That it be provided that the Governor in Council may grant an increase of one hundred dollars to any clerk in the Third Division of the Inside Service of the Civil Service and to any person holding any of the positions mentioned in section thirty-two of the Civil Service Amendment Act, 190S, who
(a)	is reported by the deputy head to be deserving of such increase; and
(b)	is in receipt of a salary of less than one thousand dollars.
I know some seventy or eighty men who have been in that division of the Civil Service for 15, 20 or 30 years, and who, by reason of their long service, have risen to the maximum of $1,200. Why should not an increase be given to such men who have been so many years in the service and who have families? I know men who are receiving only $1,200 a year, who have sons at the front, and who, by reason of the high cost of living, are really in a state of distress. Yet they cannot get any increase at all because they have reached the maximum of $1,200, while a young man without any family, or a young woman who may have been but a few years in the service, will immediately receive an increase of $100, simply because, by reason of the short period of service, bis or her salary is less than $1,000. Why is that distinction made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
The reason is that the man who has been those years-in the service receives a salary of $1,200, which, having regard to conditions outside, is a fairly substantial emolument. We are dealing with cases of hardship which arise in the Civil Service in cases of salaries under $1,000. If a man is receiving $1,200 a year he is 'better than a man who is receiving $700. There is more reason for granting an increase to a man who has only $700 a year than there is for granting an increase to a man who has $1,200 a year. My hon. friend is mistaken in his assertion that the man with a salary of $1,200 gets no increase.- We have increased the maximum from $1,200 to $1,300.
Mr. PUG8LEY: He does not receive that immediately?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: He will receive the annual increase this year. That is another point in connection with the service, and it answers the question that has been raised: Why not an increase over the whole service? It must not he overlooked that under the provisions of the Civil Service Act those who are in the first division, with a salary from $2,100 to $4,000, receive an annual increase of $100; that is, the man with $2,100 this year gets $2,200 next year, and every year he is $100 better off in salary.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Where is that provided in the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: It is in the Act, which is not affected b'y this resolution.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: I thought it was $50.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: It is $100 in the first division, and $50 in the lower divisions. My hon. friend has referred to what he regards as the extraordinary anomaly of some members of the Civil Service receiving both military ^nd civil pay, while others receive only their Civil Service salary if that is greater than the amount of military pay they would draw, and he also referred to the latest Order^m Council. I am unable to speak authoritatively at the present time with regard to that Order in Council.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
would bring it down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
I would suggest that my hon. friend ask the Prime Minister with regard to that Order in Council; it is not immediately under consideration by the committee. With regard to the other two classes, when the war broke out we decided that those who enlisted from the Civil Service should receive both their civil and military pay. That was a generous action on the part of the Government, possibly over-generous, but I think at that time nobody imagined the war would extend over such a long period, or would develop on the scale it has. Many of the large companies in this country did the same thing. I think it was not believed by any one that our expeditionary force would grow from 30,000 to 50,000, to 200,000, to
300,000,	to 400,000, or 500,000. Having regard to the size of the expeditionary force which it was then thought we should send overseas, the. Government thought it proper at that time to do what many of the large companies were doing, namely to pay those who enlisted their full civil pay in addition to their military pay. Afterwards, when recruiting went on on the scale it did, we came to the conclusion that the civil servant would be put more on a par with those outside if he was paid only the amount of his civil pay, if that should be in.excess of his military pay. That appeared to be a fair dealing with the situation, and the expense runs into a very substantial sum of money indeed. That was the position up to the time the Order in Council was passed which my hon. friend has referred to, and about which I suggested that he speak to the Prime Minister, as I am not sufficiently familiar with its terms myself.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would ask the Prime Minister. He is nearer to him than I am.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: I do not wish to discuss the Order in Council now, as it is net immediately before the House, but I _ will have no objection at all to bringing his suggestion before the Prime Minister.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: I thought that perhaps the Minister of Finance, being so prominent a member of the Government, might be able to get the Order in Council with less difficulty than I could, as it would take some time to get it by a formal motion. There are undoubtedly very great anomalies in regard to the pay of enlisted civil servants, and I think it is important that we should have this Order in Council.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
As one of the members representing the city of

Ottawa, where a large number of ladies and gentlemen are employed in the Civil Service, I desire to offer my thanks to the Government as well as to the Minister of Finance for their determination to do something to assist the civil servants, especially those of the lower grades. I think the proposal of the Minister of Finance is a fairly generous one, but I am sorry that he has not seen fit to increase the minimum salaries, especially in sub-division B of the third division, and also the salaries of messengers, porters, sorters, packers and such like. I think the minimum salary should have been made $600 or $700 instead of $500.
I wish to say a few words regarding the repeal of subsection of 2 of section 26 of the Civil Service Amendment Act of 1908. Personally, I have always looked upon that subsection, not merely as a hardship, but even a cruel measure, against the men who had been working in that class for many years. When that Act was put into force the men who had passed the qualifying examination were debarred from further promotion because they were unable to pass an academic examination such as few men in this House could pass without long preparation, and I am exceedingly glad that this subsection is going to be repealed.
I also hope the Minister of Finance will not overlook the claims of the men and' women of the Outside Service, who are working for a very low salary, and are certainly entitled to as much consideration as members of the lower grades of the inside service. I am sure the Outside Service here and elsewhere are performing their duties just ae efficiently as are the members of the Inside Service, and I venture to hope that the Government and the Minister of Finance will not overlook their just claim for an increase. They have to live in the same place as the inside servants, and the high cost of living affects them just as much as it does the inside-servants.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
A civil servant
who joined the first contingent would get both civil and military pay. Will this increase apply to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
Does- not the minister
think that will cause some ill feeling? There may be two men side by side, one getting only the military pay and the other both military pay and say $1,200 a year. Now the Government proposes to increase the pay of the man who is getting $1,200-

more than the man beside him, and does not increase the other man's pay. That does not seem to one to be reasonable, and I think it will cause a great deal of dissatisfaction. Those civil servants who first enlisted are getting quite a big bonus over those who enlisted later. This seems to be a case of "For he that hath to him shall be given; and he that hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he hath."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
Personally I do
not like to deprive any soldier of any emolument that he is receiving at the ^present time. There is this to be said for those who are receiving double pay. These men went forward on that understanding, and it does not seem to me that it would be just or proper to revise the conditions under which they enlisted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: No one is suggesting that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
After all, I do
not think the public interest is likely to suffer if these men who went forward with the first contingent, or shortly afterwards, and are in receipt of the double pay, are given a little more than possibly what on a strict business basis they might be entitled to. The same remark would apply to those who went forward on the understanding they would get their civil pay if that were in excess of their military pay. To meet the point raised toy my hon. friend, aJbout having to go to the deputy to obtain this increase, I would be willing so far as I am concerned to amend subsection A of section 3 if in the opinion of the committee any hardship is likely to result therefrom, and allow the Governor in Council to grant the increase upon the recommendation of the minister. If there is any considerable opinion in favour of it, on the part of the committee, I am willing that this should be done, but I believe that the matter is in good hands, that the Act will be administered fairly, and that no hardship will result.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: The minister evidently misunderstood the tenor of my remarks. I do not want to prevent the man who comes under the Order in Council from getting an increase. But why not give an increase to the man beside him, who is getting from $600 to $1,200 less? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: That does not arise under this resolution.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
This Government seldom does anything that pleases me, and when it
does I feel like making note of it. I am not sure that the Civil Service Act has hampered this Government as much as it hampered its predecessor. I find, for instance, that section 21 has been overworked by this Government. That is the section that provides that a person may enter the Civil Service without passing an examination, on the ground of having some technical qualifications. The action taken by the minister in allowing civil servants to be promoted from one class to another without passing an examination which he calls "academic," I think, is a good one, particularly as it applies to the old employees. A good deal of nonsense is . talked about Civil Service examinations-at least I think so. I always imagined, until I was enlightened on the subject by a few months' practical observation, that promotions would largely remain as they were and would be made on the recommendation of the deputy minister. Speaking practically, if I had my way, promotions should be altogether upon the recommendation of the deputy, he acting on the recommendation of the head of the branch in which the civil servant is employed. It is all very well to have an examination, but it may be that the individual who is least competent to pass an academic examination may be the one best fitted from the practical point of view for promotion. The same applies in any business; any one can apply it in his own office. While, generally speaking, it is better to have a high standard of education, yet education and practical qualifications are not always united in the same person. I found that in several cases when I was in charge of a department. The person who could pass the examination had to have the promotion, while the one who could not pass the examination . was, to my mind, better qualified for the position. "But," you say, "will that remove political pull and influence?" There must be a certain amount of confidence in a department, just as in a business establishment. The deputy minister must be a man in whom the Government and the public have confidence, one as well able to judge of the ability of officers of the department as the heads of branches under whom they work. Not many agree with me, perhaps, but I would go so far as to say that all promotions ought to be on recommendation, not of the minister, but of the head of the branch, countersigned and approved by the deputy minister. My hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) rather thinks

that this power should be removed from the deputies. I think if he were at the head of a department, or sat at the council board for a time, he would change his mind.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: The hon. member misunderstood my views. I think the minimum salary should be fixed.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
I was referring to promotion, not salaries. A member of tl)e Government is human; the members of this Government are exceptionally human so far as their friends are concerned. I am afraid that if the two members from Ottawa, whom I see here to-day and working very hard, both attacked the minister at once the minister could hardly repel them, he could hardly withstand their seductive influence. If the authority were in the minister's hands, he might suggest-the promotion of an individual whom the deputy would not recommend on his or her qualifications. Leave it in the hands of the deputy minister, and it will be near enough to the minister, while at the same time the minister will not be liable to the charge of exercising political preference as he would be if the matter were left in his own hands.
'Mr. CHA130T: I would go further than the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). I believe it would be in the interests of the country if the civil servants, Inside and Outside Services, were entirely under the control of commissions and beyond the pale of politics, both in regard to appointment and promotion.	,

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
I have had some experience, as hon. members know, with regard to the Civil Service. I agree with the hon. member for South Renfrew that it would be the greatest mistake in the world to do away with the recommendation of the deputy minister. It would mean that the members for Ottawa for the time being would be deluged with requests from members of the Civil Service. I believe that it is in the interest of the Civil Service that promotions should be made on the recommendation of the deputy minister. My five years' experience leads me to believe that it would be in the interest of the Service if the civil servants were removed from politics and disfranchised. That is my judgment. If the minister would go that far, and not allow the civil servant to* vote or have any interest in the country politically, I think it would be to the interest of the civil servants as well as to the interest of the country at large: At present, there is a certain influence unnecessarily brought to bear on
[Mr. Graham, [	~
the members that I think should be avoided. I certainly think that the resolution, on the whole, is in the interests of the civil servant as well as of the country. Let the deputy minister recommend the increases. I am sure the civil servant himself [vill be perfectly satisfied to allow that recommendation to decide whether he is entitled to the increase or not. With regard to the members of the Third Division whp are to be promoted without passing an academic examination, there are between four and five hundred men who have reached the maximum of their class and cannot get out of that division, and who are earning $1,200 a year. They have certainly been under great hardship for some years past, particularly since the high cost of living has attacked us all. We all know that the man on salary is particularly hard hit by the increased prices. Another point to be remembered is that the civil servants cannot, like our trades unions, demand increases; they must depend altogether upon the generosity of the government of the day. I hope the House will accept the resolution as it stands. I am sure it will be acceptable to the Civil Service and that they will do their duty all the better as civil servants in consequence of the -legislation that it is now proposed to pass.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
I also am in
favour of the Civil Service of this country, both inside and outside, being taken absolutely out of politics and put under the administration of a commission. I believe that all recommendations as to the promotions of civil servants should come from that commission and that there should be no outside influence as to appointment, promotion or anything else. I was under the impression that we had attained that some years ago when what we considered to be a sweeping Ao$ was put through this House and we established a Civil Service Commission of some character. Just what it is now, I do not know. But I am convinced that public opinion is in favour of taking the Civil Service, outside and inside, away from political influence and putting it in the hands of a board, non-political in character. I believe that appointments and promotions should be made absolutely from the point of view of the Civil Service, and I believe in treating fairly and paying decently those wlm are in the service. I believe that reasonable promotion ought to be provided for and that when promotion does take place it should be on merit and on the recommendation of a responsible officer of the department,.such as the deputy

minister or the officer in charge of the branch.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
There is just one word I
wish to add to this discussion. The idea of putting the service entirely under a commission is all right, but there is one objection to it as the system is carried out now. I think that the Government should take steps to see that appointments to the Civil Service are more equitably distributed. I have no objection to my hon. friends from Ottawa getting a fair proportion of the appointments, but -as nearly as I can make out sixty or seventy per cent of the appointments to the Civil Service in Ottawa-and now it ie getting worse-it is eighty or eighty-five per cent-are of people belonging to the city of Ottawa. There are other men and women in other parts of the country who are entitled to a look-in in the service. I took up the' matter of finding out who were in the Inside Service when the patronage of my. riding came under my purview, and on looking over the whole list I found that there had been just one man appointed to the Inside Service from North Simcoe in thirty years. I have no doubt there are other ridings in a similar position. I do not believe in this policy of the pork barrel, especially when the hand that goes into the pork barrel is only one hand, but I think we ought all to get a fair trial and that some new rule should be adopted by the different departments so that young men and women, and especially returned soldiers from other parts of the country outside of Ottawa might have a fair share of the jobs in the Inside Service.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: The finest Civil Service in the world is the Indian Civil Service and appointment to it is altogether by examination. There ie no such thing as recommendation. The most influential man in England could not get an appointment to, or promotion in, the Indian Civil Service unless he passed the examination and got the proper standing. The door is open to the least influential person in the country if he has brains, aptitude and fitness. This business of recommendation is absurd. That there should be a difference between the conduct of the Inside and Outside Service is something that I cannot understand at all. Surely it is only reasonable that a commission should be allowed, without regard to partisanship or political preference, or anything of that sort, to manage the affairs of the service in such a way that those whose ability and fitness are indicated by their examinations should receive the preference. It seems to me strange that it should have been taken for granted that an examination must be on some abstruse mathematical problem or some extraordinary question in geography or history that a person might not be able to answer although he might have the aptitude and business for the work he undertakes. The examination ought to be of such a character as to have some reference to the man's employment. Surely it is not beyond the power of human brains to launch something of that sort. At any rate, we are not following out the best examples in other countries where the system has been worked out satisfactorily. It cannot be said that political recommendations by members for the Inside or the Outside Service-of course it is not for Inside Servio now-are in any sense to the advantage of the country.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
Of all the absurdities of the present system one of the most conspicuous is that the men who happen to be the members for Ottawa should have the patronage of recommending people for appointments to a great service that should draw its candidates from all parts of the Dominion. We are creating by this partisan and political system a professional class of civil servants resident in the Capital. The service is administered largely on the recommendation of the local members and not with regard to the public interest. Again I desire to say that it is high time, especially in these critical war times when we wish to get value for every dollar that is voted by this House, that the administration of the Civil Service, outside and in, should be absolutely non-partisan and should be in the hands of a competent commission, and should not be the subject of political patronage. I am prepared to endorse what has been said by the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) in regard to the Indian Service, from the very limited knowledge I have of it. Everybody knows that in England they have a much better administration of the public service than we have here, that the examinations are fair, that there is reasonable promotion, and that, most important of all, those in the service are not discouraged by the knowledge that unfair preference will be given to another member of the service by reason of political influence. That is the most disheartening thing in a service of this kind. By political influence people can get preference, better salaries and advancement over those who are perhaps doing better work but who have not the necessary political influence. Surely,

it is time to bring all this to an end and instead of patching up this Act as we are doing now-and it is only being patched up now in order to do justice to the lower grades of the service-we should take the service out of politics and put it in the hands of a commission where it will be fairly and justly administered. The commission should present to Parliament, or to the minister, a report reviewing the whole condition of the service, suggesting improvements and, if in times like this they think it is necessary to increase the pay of the service, recommending it to us. This would be an intelligent way of dealing with the matter.	'

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words in reply to the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) and the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean). I am sure they are labouring under a misapprehension in so far as the political power and authority of the Ottawa members is concerned. They could not at all have exaggerated, if they had attempted to describe, the tribulations and vicissitudes that we have to undergo with regard to the duties to be performed in connection with the appointment and recommendation of men and women to the Outside Service only. We have nothing to do with appointments to or promotions in the Inside Service than any other hon. member of this House because since 1908 all appointments to and promotions in the Inside Service are supposed to be made by the Civil Service Commission.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext:
That word "supposed" is a good qualification.
Mr. C'HABOT:	Not only "supposed"
but should be made by the Civil Service Commission, which was appointed by the late Government. With regard to outside appointments, probably the Outside Service in Ottawa is more varied and more extensive than it is in any other constituency in Canada and that may toe the cause of so much trouble for the gentlemen who happen to represent this city when their party is in power. As I said, I agree with the hon. member for York (Mr. W. P. Maclean) that all civil services should be directly and absolutely under Civil Service Commissions, either under the present Commission, numerically increased, or a separate Commission outside of politics altogether. If that were done I am satisfied that this country would get a more efficient service.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: If it is put forward that these promotions are to be political, I would keep a party ledger and I would make it the duty of the whips of the party in power to keep a ledger for each constituency, having regard to the population of the constituency.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Why not the card index system ?

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: Hold on nowand I would say that it would be their duty to see that outlying counties get their share of this patronage, if it is to be patronage. So I protest against it on two grounds, not only do I think it unfair and that it should not exist, but if that system is to be maintained, it should toe maintained on the basis of a fair distribution of these offices among the outyling constituencies as well as in the large centres, like Toronto, where there is a great deal of patronage in connection with the Outside Service. A large portion of that Post Office patronage might toe fairly distributed to other ridings adjacent to that city. I do not advocate either of these things. I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chabot) that the Outside Service should be taken out of politics and administered by a Comission.

subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD DIVISIONS OF THE SERVICE
speechtext: I should like tp emphasize the remarks made by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) that the Civil Service should be disfranchised. That is a position that I have taken ever since I have been a member of this_ House. It seems to me that there is no good reason why they should not he disfranchised. The proposal to disfranchise the Civil Service is repugnant to me as taking away from th.e liberty of the citizen. Simply because a man happens to be working for the Government is no reason why he should not have the right to vote. There are two ways, however, of disfranchising civil servants: one by taking away their vote, and the other by muzzling them. A practice was in force-I hope it will not be continued at the next election-of dismissing a man simply because he voted for one party or for another. I have in mind instances of investigation into the conduct of officials, who were suspended or dismissed if their conduct did not tally exactly with the party view. In reading over the report of an investigation which took place in my county-I wish to speak particularly of matters of which I have certain knowledge-I found that a certain gentleman said to a friend whom he had in his drawing-room one evening after a meeting, that after all he thought Laurier was not a bad fellow. That is all he said; that was all that was brought out before the investigating commissioner. Had he said that I was or was not a bad fellow, and that, accordingly, he should or should not vote for me, I would not mind; but it seems absurd that he should lose his position simply because he said that the leader of a party was not a bad fellow. .That is what I call muzzling the civil servant and, therefore, disfranchising him; because if you take away his position by reason of his having voted a certain way, in effect you practically take away his vote. [Mr. Pugsley.J

subtopic: PROPOSED MINISTRY OP FISHERIES.
speechtext:
That all the words after "that" he struck out and the following substituted therefor: "In the opinion of this House, in view of the food shortage with which this country is confronted, and for the purpose of materially increasing the resources and food supply of Canada, a Department of Fisheries, under a separate minister, should be forthwith organized.
He said: It is obviously the duty of any member of this House to bring to the attention of the Government and of the country any project the adoption of which he conscientiously believes will add to the resources .or food supply of Canada during the serious years with which we are confronted. This being so, I desire to present to the House very briefly the opinion which I enr tertain regarding the absolutely essential action to be taken by this Government in order to render vastly more productive an important source of food 'supply, namely, the fisheries of this country.
For many years the reports which successive ministers have laid upon the table of this House have reiterated the statement that the fisheries of Canada are the most extensive in the world. So far as possibilities are concerned, that statement is absolutely correct. The geographical position of Canada in that respect is unsurpassed.
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
But, in so far as results are concerned, the departmental statement is, unfortunately, entirely misleading. If we consider the value of the product of fisheries of certain .other countries, we find the following. I give the results in round numbers, because I am no more fond of statistics than is this House:
United States	$76,000,000
Great Britain (before the war) ..	75,000,000
Norway, in 1915	 50,000,000
Japan	 4-5,000,000
Canada, in 1916	 35,860,000
Looking more closely at the reports of the Canadian fisheries, we find the following results:
Value
of Products.
1896	$20,470,000
1916 	 35,860,000
The increase of 75 per cent on the face of it, might perhaps appeal to the casual reader of the report as being fairly satisfactory. But, it is a fact-I do not know how broadly it is recognized-that within the same twenty years the average market value of Canadian sea foods

has advanced over 67 per cent. Consequently the increase in' the production of sea foods of Canada within that time has ibeen rather less than 8 per cent, which is much more than inade up by the increase in the quantity of salmon taken in the British Columbia fisheries. The capital invested in the fisheries in 1896 was $9,826,000 and in 1916 it was $25,-
855,000,	and the cost of operation has proportionately increased during the same period. In other words, it has been of late years costing us $2.50 to produce the same quantity of sea foods that in 1896 we produced at an expenditure of $1.
It is not a pleasant thing to contemplate, but it is a fact, nevertheless, that in so far as production is concerned, the fisheries of Canada have practically stood still during the past twenty years. This has been due, in the main, to four things-lack of attention, lack of appreciation, lack of vision, and lack of intelligent, progressive policy. Instead of $35,000,000, the fisheries of Canada should to-day be yielding $60,000,000, * and in five years they could 'be made to produce $100,000,000 annually. We all remember, not so very many years ago, when the wheat fields of the West first yielded a $100,000,000 harvest. What a great shout went up from the people of the country, and how the newspapers, East and West, commented on the splendid achievement. But, we had waited 25 years and had expended hundreds of millions of dollars in building railways and elevators to make that result possible. Are -not $100,000,000 drawn from the harvest of the seas of equal economical value to this country? Mr. Speaker, they are not only equal but more so, because the wheat fields of the West require cultivation, while the sea fisheries do not. Why have we not recognized and profited by that obvious fact? The reason is because the fisheries have always been neglected; because they are to-day, and havie been for years, a mere adjunct of the Naval Service Department, which in turn, is an adjunct of the Marine and Fisheries Department under one minister. No man, even though he be a demi-god, could successfully conduct the fisheries of Canada as at present organized. One naturally asks why this is so. Sir, the answer is not far to seek. In the first place, how is the time of a minister of the Crown occupied? Let us take the case of a reasonably industrious minister; one who spends six out of the seven days of the week toiling away in his office in the Capital. One full day at least
of the week is occupied in answering correspondence; one full day in the week is occupied in receiving delegations and callers; two full days in the week are occupied at Council attending to matters pertaining to other departments; one day in the week, perhaps, is devoted to matters of general policy, and, possibly, politics; while if this House is in session, one full day in the week is spent in this Chamber, leaving at .best one full day in the week devoted to attending to the special duties appertaining to his department. I would like to digress just for one moment to point out ' that, aside from agriculture, the chief items of our annual production in raw material in 1915 were:

Coal	 32,111,000

Pulpwood	  15,590,000

Pig iron from Canadian ore .. ..	1,715,000
Being for the most part under provincial control and under the especial care of many provincial departments of Government, they were in the main very well cared for. The fisheries of Canada yield $35,000,000, according to the departmental blue books, and in what relation do they stand to the Federal Department of Marine and Fisheries? Let us turn to the list of services in that jdepart-ment, and we will find that they number 37, of which the fisheries is one. I think I should read the list:

Which of these 37 services of the department is it that occupies the minister's one available day of the week? The fisheries, as I have pointed out, is the one single productive service in the department. Do you suppose the fisheries get the minister's one available day for the week? If you will excuse me the expression, the fisheries do not get a "look-in." Who looks after the fisheries branch? Not the minister, because the minister has not the time; not the deputy minister, because his 'time is otherwise fully occupied. It is the superintendent of fisheries, a man with little authority, and a man who cannot make any recommendation in the matter of policy, I venture to say, unless specially requested to do so. In any case his time is fully occupied by the thousand and one details of his department which arise daily. Hence the fisheries do not get, and cannot get, fair play in the department, and, in my opinion, they do not get fair play in this House. Few members take any interest in them, while the discussion of any matter pertaining to the fisheries is the signal generally for a thinning out in the attendance of this Chamber. Let me give an illustration. Last year, upon a resolution introduced by myself, a committee was appointed to investigate the spread in price of sea foods in Canada. That committee held twelve sittings. The minister never attended a single session of the committee. I am quite prepared to admit that his time was otherwise fully occupied. The deputy minister never attended a single sitting of the committee, and I am prepared to admit that his time also was fully occupied. The superintendent of fisheries was there and rendered excellent service, but, as I have pointed out, he has no authority. That committee made a report which was presented to this House. That report was to have been discussed on the last day of the session along with the reports of the committees on pensions and public printing. That was the arrangement; I made it myself with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine. But it was never carried out, because the first named committee, quite unnecessarily I think, occupied almost every moment of the time.

I repeat, therefore, that the fisheries of Canada, which could be made to produce $100,000,000 per annum, have been neglected and ignored for years; both by the department and this House. Just here I will make the observation, if I may be permitted, that my experience in this House has forced me to the conclusion that economic questions do not invite that consideration to which I think they are entitled. That has probably been due to the fact that our political problems have been vexed and perplexing, and that the natural wealth of the country has been great and its development rapid, if not feverish. But the time is coming, if, indeed, it is not already here, when economic questions will engage the attention of this Parliament, and when mere questions of party and of the respective and relative advantages of the "ins" and the "outs" will be pressed back into second place. There are those in this country who desire to see the Dominion rounded out by bringing Newfoundland into the Confederation family. The ancient colony has not hitherto shown any great anxiety for the union, and I am not certain that she can even be induced to become a war bride.	Many
reasons are given for her indifference in this respect, but I think at the heart of it all is the fact that the great majority of the male population of Newfoundland are engaged in the fisheries, that almost $11,000,000 of her annual export of $14,000,000 is derived from the fisheries. They are opposed to Confederation, I think, because they say Our fisheries have advanced while those of Canada have practically stood still; why should we exchange a policy of progress, development and growth for one which is just the reverse? And why is it that the fisheries of Canada are in that unhappy position? The reason is that they have never had the first care and attention of the head of the department nor, under present conditions, will they ever get it and the two problems of economical production and economical distribution have been unsolved. In this condition of affairs one naturally asks, what is the remedy, what can be done? In my opinion there should be organized a Department of Fisheries with a separate minister responsible to this House and to this country. The fisheries of Canada are surely big enough and exten- >
sive enough and important enough to warrant this. A Minister of Fisheries would find his time fully occupied for several years to come in grappling with and solving of the two great problems of economical production

and economical distribution of sea foods in this country. Such action is furthermore necessary in order to reassure the fishermen and the fishing interests of this country. It is certainly necessary in order to command attention and respect for the fisheries of this country in this House. Above all things it is necessary in order to secure respect for the fisheries and the fishing interests from the transportation companies and concerns operating in Canada. So long as the present system is continued the present conditions will prevail, and this country will fail to reap tens of millions of dollars which might, under proper conditions, be drawn from the har-. vests of the sea. I am not charging this Government with especial negligence in this matter. They are merely following, or I might say perpetuating, the policy which they found upon coming into office, a policy which, indeed, has been pursued by all governments more or less indifferently since Confederation. But, Sir, to-day with the highest authorities gravely assuring us that the world's food supply will be seriously impaired during the years which are even now upon us; with Professor Cudmore of Toronto University pointing to the fact that the world's wheat harvest of last year was about 960,000,000 bushels less than the year before with men of the calibre of Lord Shaughnessy telling us that if we are to survive economically we must get out of the habit of thinking and acting in ruts; with the hon. the Minister of Finance praying for greater economy on the one hand and the hon. the Minister of Trade and Cominerce preaching increased production on the other, I say, with this array of unquestionable testimony before us as to the necessity of the hour, would it not be little short of criminal for us to stand idly by and fail to avail ourselves of the almost unlimited supply of sea foods at our very door? We cannot do it organized as we are; we can do it by proper organization wdthout involving additional expense. Therefore I say to this Government, as to men charged with the gravest responsibilities, organize a Department of Fisheries, place the portfolio in the hands of a man of ability, courage and vision, from within this House or from outside of it, I care not which, nor am I particular as to what his political antecedents may be-and support him in carrying out a policy which is calculated to meet the national requirements.

subtopic: PROPOSED MINISTRY OP FISHERIES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to second the motion of the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson),
I wish to say a very few words. It is not my intention to quote any statistics or to go into any details in the general argument or suggestions which I purpose making. First, I wish to emphasize and to support the statements of the mover of the resolution as to the food value of fish. I think the food value of fish is now admitted by all, and the only thing that we lack in this country is a due appreciation of the quantity of this food material that lies at our doors,ready for use and proper exploitation. My hon. friend has pointed out that the annual fish production of Canada, which is valued at approximately $35,000,000, can be doubled, and, perhaps, trebled. There is no question that fish is an excellent substitute for meat, the cost of which has so abnormally increased. A movement was recently set on foot in the Motherland to increase the consumption of fish with a view to reducing the consumption of meat and helping to bring about that economy which is so necessary under present conditions. That fish, therefore, is of great value as a food cannot be disputed, and my hon. friend deserves commendation for bringing to the attenion of the House the matter of the exploitation of our fisheries.	'
The administration of the fisheries is practically an appendage of the Marine and Fisheries Department. I would not for a moment reflect upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries by saying that the Fisheries Branch of his department is not properly administered. Without question, the minister has given his best services to that work, so far as he has 'been able to do so. But many matters of importance come under the jurisdiction of the Marine and Fisheries Department. There is the control and direction <?f navigation in Canada, a matter of very great importance indeed. The matter of pilotage is also an important one, the regulations in connection with which require constant revision and supervision. The administering of the great harbours and their foreshores is also part of the duty of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. These matters, together with the administration of naval affairs, now occupy a very large part of the minister's time. I do not think that the House, or the country, expect one minister to assume a task that is beyond the capabilities of one man. That principle was recognized by the House; it has been recognized since war broke out by the appointment of an assistant to the Minister of Militia and of another, I think, to the Minister of Finance. I am not suggesting that in this case an under-secretary

would fill the hill, (because the administration of the fisheries is sufficient to occupy the full time of a minister appointed for that special purpose.
Another thing which must not be forgotten, is that Great Britain built up her position as a naval power upon the fisher-folk of the British Isles, who form the first line of defence of the United Kingdom, as the fishermen here form our first line of defence in Canada. A few years ago the Maritime Provinces, and particularly the province of Nova Scotia, contributed to the seafaring element of our population the finest class of men produced by any nation. Two or three years ago, sixty-five per cent of the captains sailing in and out of the port of Vancouver came from the province of Nova Scotia. Through the failure of the governments of Canada during the last thirty or forty years to take steps in regard to the matter-I am referring now more particularly to governments preceding this one, though the condition still prevails to some extent-the fisheries of the coast have passed largely into the hands of Japanese or foreigners. Twenty years ago one would see scarcely a single Japanese fishing in northern British Columbia or north of the Fraser river, but to-day a large majority of those fishing on the Pacific coast are Japanese. It is not my desire to reflect on the Japanese, but I contend that it is the duty of Parliament and of the people to conserve Ifor British citizens, native-born if possible, this valuable franchise of the right to fish.

speechtext:
The minister's suggestion is quite right, but the point is that these people have become British subjects simply for the purpose of securing a fishing license. On the Pacific and Atlantic coasts the fisherfolk form, as I have said, our first line of defence, and if you build up a strong, intelligent and prosperous community of fishermen along our coasts, the result will be an immense benefit to the country not only in the way of production, but also in the way of defence in time of war. A commander of one of the British cruisers a few months ago told me that when he was in the service on the Canadian. Atlantic coast there passed through his hands several hundred recruits from the Maritime Provinces and Newfoundland who were as fine a class of men as could foe found. I mention this merely to show the value of these

men to the country. The greatest service is being rendered to the Mother Country to-day by mine sweepers in the seas surrounding Great Britain, manned by the crews of the trawlers of England's great fishing fleet. This will impress the House with the necessity of building up the fishing communities on our sea coast and the undesirability of allowing our fisheries to drift into the control of aliens or of nationalities that are not as sympathetic with us as we should like. I do not wish to criticise the minister of the department, but I do submit that our fisheries are of sufficient importance to justify the establishing of a separate department for their administration, that department to be in charge of a minister of the Crown. Not only would this be a step in the interest of the production and distribution of food, but it would build up among the fisherfolk along our coasts a race that will maintain the traditions of the fisherfolk of our Empire.
