speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: PROPOSED MINISTRY OP FISHERIES.
speechtext:
I stated the other evening that it was my intention when the Fisheries' Estimates came before the House, to make a statement regarding the activities and progress of the department during the past year. It was suggested by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) last year, that I should make such a statement, and I always like to accept a good suggestion no matter where it comes from. In view of the fact that the fisheries .question has been brought before the House this afternoon by my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) on the motion to go into Supply, it occurred to me that this might be even a more fitting time to make the statement that when the Fisheries' Estimates come before the House. I think this is especially desirable in view of the fact that the Marine and Fisheries Committee after a number of meetings during last session made a report to the House which contained many valuable suggestions.
I regret to say that I was not able last year to attend the meetings of that committee, for the reason that in addition to the work of my own department which, according to the hon. member for Digby, embraces almost 37 departments, I had thrown upon my shoulders during the session the work of the Department of Agriculture to a con-

siderable extent, as the Minister of Agriculture was suffering from injuries sustained during the burning of the Parliament buildings. In addition to that I was also acting as chairman of the Pensions Committee. With all these duties on my shoulders, I regret to say that I found it impossible to attend the meetings of the Marine and Fisheries Committee last year. As I have said they made a very valuable report to the House, and their suggestions have been given every consideration by the department, and I propose now to let the House know just what action we have taken in regard to them, before discussing more particularly what was said by my hon. friend from Digby and my hon. friend from Vancouver City (Mr. Stevens) this afternoon.
Unfortunately it is still no easy task to afford adequate protection to the fisheries that require it. Hence, a great deal of the department's work is essentially of a negative character. While this work is of the utmost importance, and is exacting on time, the affirmative side,-the doing of things to increase the knowledge of the fishermen in the life history of fish, to enable them to catch more fish, to prevent them losing valuable time, to encourage the better handling of fish, so that the fishermen will get more for their catches and the public a better article of food, to provide better facilities and cheaper rates for the transportation of fish, to bring to the attention of the public the value, cheapness and general excellence of fish as food, and the keeping up and increasing of the supply of certain kinds of fish by artificial hatching-is from year to year receiving more attention.
Last session the Select Standing Committee on Marine and Fisheries made an exhaustive investigation into the spread in price of sea foods. The valuable report and recommendations and evidence procured, which were submitted by the committee to the House, will still be fresh in the minds of the members. The recommendations made have been acted on by the department, and as far as possible they have been effected. It may be best to cite the recommendations and summarize the action taken thereon. The first recommendation was:
1.	That inspection of transportation of sea foods, and organization of the distribution thereof, be undertaken by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, somewhat along the lines already inaugurated by the Department of Agriculture in respect to certain farm products.
A young man, Mr. Leonard, of St. John, who has been brought up in the fish business, and who is consequently familiar with the requirements in transportation, was appointed inspector on the 1st July last, and was continued in such position until the end of September. His headquarters were at Mulgrave, Nova Scotia. The Canadian Government railways did everything they could to facilitate his work, including furnishing him with transportation, good for express or freight trains, so that he was not only in a position to see and direct the handling of shipments of fresh fish at the very important shipping and transhipping point, but was enabled to accompany shipments from place to place and see the conditions at other important shipping points. On the whole he found conditions fairly satisfactory. Following suggestions made by him, the railway arranged to make some improvements for the icing of refrigerator freight cars and the marking of such cars on the outside so as to minimize the danger of their being disconnected from the train at switching points, and so delayed in reaching their destination. It will be remembered that it was regarded by some as necessary that refrigerator express cars should be available for local shipments as well as for through shipments. Experiments made by the inspector proved this not to be so. Fish packed in a liberal supply of ice reached their destination to points in the Maritime Provinces in perfect condition when forwarded in ordinary express cars. It is not considered that it will be necessary to again employ an inspector, at least for the present. The second and third recommendations were:
2.	That the express facilities be so improved as to insure daily transportation of sea foods from the east by means of the chilled car service.
3.	That the refrigerator ear service for the transportation of sea foods be so improved as to render it available on express trains.
In order that the conditions and requirements might be most perfectly understood by both sides, last spring a conference was called by the department of representatives of the, railways, express companies and fish merchants. It was of a highly satis-i factory nature, and resulted in a clear understanding of the difficulties on both sides. The railway undertook to overcome as far as possible, the obstacles to the more general use of the refrigerator fast freight service, and though it has made consistent earnest efforts in that direction, it must not be overlooked that the movement of

troops and war equipment has necessarily seriously handicapped such efforts.
The putting on of a refrigerator express service was subsequently taken up with the manager of the Canadian Government railways. It was found that the existing refrigerator cars are really not safe for use on fast passenger trains, and apart from the undue cost of new cars at the present time, they could not be speedily built. It was arranged, however, that the railway would insulate a portion of one of its large express baggage cars for fish transportation and run a *weekly refrigerator service from Mulgrave to Montreal, shipments from Halifax being consolidated at Truro, and if it transpired that this was used to such an extent as to require additional space, further cars would be so arranged. This service was in operation up to the end of November. While it was the best that could be done at that time, it has not proved fully satisfactory. Apart from the lack of proper rolling stock, the heavy loading of the passenger trains involves serious difficulties. Were the express shipments and mails sufficient to warrant special trains, the difficulty would be minimized. This question is being kept in the forefront by *the department.
The fourth recommendation was:
That the consolidation of shipments for different points in the express refrigerator car, on the basis of carload express rates, to the farthest point, and the opening of car in transit to set down fish at different centres en route, would materially aid prompt and economical distribution of sea foods.
The express companies, after full consideration of this recommendation, intimated that they are unable to comply with it.
The fifth recommendation was:
That a carload lot express rate, substantially lower than the L.C.L. rate, should be fixed on sea foods from the east.
The companies maintain that the existing L.C.L. rate is as low as a C.L. rate should be, and that they therefore cannot reduce it.
The sixth recommendation was:
That the minimum freight carload quantity, on the Government railway be reduced from a new scale of 24,000 pounds to the former scale of 20,000' pounds, in the case of fresh sea foods, and from the new scale of 30,000 pounds to the former scale of 24,000 pounds in the case of cured sea foods.
The railway agreed to do this, and it was put into effect early last summer.
The seventh recommendation was:
That transportation companies should give special attention to the movement of cars con-
	*
taining perishable food commodities, to secure delivery thereof without deterioration.
This matter was taken up with the railways, and, as previously indicated, in fast freight shipments the cars are being specially marked on the outside, and every care is to be taken of express shipments.
The eighth recommendation was:
That an exclusive express service operated by the Government be inaugurated on the Intercolonial Railway and Prince Edward Island sections of the Government railways, as a preliminary to any general scheme for the nationalization of express business In Canada.
As this is a matter for the Railway Department in the first instance, it was referred to the minister of that department, who will no doubt be in a position to state what conclusion has been reached.
The ninth recommendation was:
That the fish diet be made a special feature on the Intercolonial dining cars, the price not to exceed the cost and expense of serving the same, as shown by the evidence.
(Note.) This would be In line with the policy of certain important railways which make a special feature of food products peculiar to the country traversed by such railways, tending to increase the consumption and- advertise the product.
While the Intercolonial Railway has not made a low rate on fish in its dining ears, it is specializing on fish, and calling attention to it by special menu cards.
The tenth recommendation was:
That an active publicity campaign be organized by a competent person to promote an increased demand for sea food in Canada.
In view of the fact that the demand for fish is expanding so rapidly as to make production a real problem, it was considered best to defer action on this matter for the present.
The eleventh recommendation was:
That the department have made, for demonstration purposes:	(a) An inexpensive refrigeration box, suitable for use in retail fish stores, in which fresh fish can he attractively displayed without, risk of deterioration; and (b) a portable refrigerator, suitable for use in the distribution of sea foods in towns and cities; and that plans and specifications thereof, with estimate .of cost, be furnished by the department upon application.
After considerable experimenting the department devised a cheap but attractive and efficient showcase. The names of companies in different parts of the country prepared to manufacture it, and the prices, were procured and pamphlets descriptive of it were prepared and distributed to the trade, and intimating that on

application the names and prices of such companies would be given or, if preferred, working plans and specifications would be furnished free to any one desiring to have a case built locally. The wholesale fish firm of D. Hatton 'Company of Montreal, has recently informed the department that it has 200 of these show, cases built, and that it is distributing them amongst the retail trade.
Up tp the moment no practical appliance of the character suggested, has been devised, and none can he found to be in use anywhere. The twelfth and thirteenth recommendations were:
That the existing scale of Government aid in the transportation of certain sea foods by express be for the present continued under regulations as to methods of shipments, and that the steps already taken to promote the packing of herrings by the Scotch method are approved, and that special attention be given to the development of this branch of the industry.
These have been complied with.
With regard to the improvement of lakes and other waters that have been to some extent depleted I may say that fish breeding is being extended as rapidly as feasible, and is being continuously conducted with greater efficiency. The benefits are so well known as to require no argument. The salmon rivers of the Atlantic coast are steadily improving. The 'Great Lakes were never more productive than at present. Lake Winnipeg, which some years ago was in a serious condition, is quite recovered, and has more fish than for many years past.
The Fisheries Exhibit at the Toronto Exhibition was again given last year, and a restaurant operated in connection with it. I think hon. members whp have seen this exhibit will agree that exhibit has not 'been allowed to suffer by repetition, new features being introduced each year. 'It was again awarded a gold medal. The patronage of the restaurant was limited only foy its capacity. Day after day it was necessary to close the doors 'at times. Over 37,000 meals were served during the twelve days of the fair. In the year before, the number of meals served was about, 25,000. Last year the number was 37,000 as I have stated, and had we had more accommodation, which it was impossible to procure, a still larger numlber would have been served. We believe that these meals of fish, well served in splendid condition, and at moderate prices, will have the effect .of making the value of fish as a food better known in Toronto and .in western Ontario generally. Men engaged in the fish business in Toronto have informed me that, as a consequence of
this exhibit and restaurant, their business has shown a very c.onsiderable increase during the past few years.
While the full information necessary to enalble an analysis of the fisheries for the fiscal year which has just closed is not available, one for the calendar year, which can be made up, so far as the sea fisheries are concerned, from the monthly bulletins published by the department, may be of value and interest. Apart fr.om any difference that may exist from year to year, in the number of men and vessels actually engaged in fishing, there are natural conditions which affect the volume of production and which have to be duly considered when comparing the results of one year with another. For example, our salmon production is affected by the phenomenon of a big run occurring on the Fraser river every fourth year, growing gradually less in the following years till it reaches its poorest stage in the year preceding the next big-run year. Our hook and line fisheries for such fish as cod, haddock, hake, halibut, etc., on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts are dependent on a supply of herring for bait, so that a scarcity or abundance o-f that bait fish immensely affects the output, of the line fishermen.
The dogfish is always with us,-in vaster numbers in some seasons than in others- devouring edible fish and destroying gear to such an extent as to stop operations at times. The somewhat erratic appearances of the mackerel and herring masses and fish of their kind on our coasts produce varying results from year to year. Finally, by limiting the number of fishing days, or permitting operations on the greatest possible number of days in the course pf a season, the weather conditions affect the production of all kinds of fish, perhaps more than any other natural agent.
The season of 1916 was characterized by several adverse conditions. There was a general scarcity of men, particularly on the Pacific coast, owing to enlistments; the poorest salmon year in the cycle of four on the Fraser river occurred; there was an abnormal amount of unfavourable, foggy weather on the Atlantic coast; the spring herring fishery in the Gulf of St. Lawrence was much curtailed owing to ice remaining on the coast till a late date; and the summer and fall herring fishery all over the Atlantic coast was practically a failure. Considering these adverse conditions, it is not surprising to find the production of

some of the chief kinds somewhat below that of the year before. Compared with 1913, .however,-a pre-war year,-the production of cod, haddock, etc., and such fish as remain fairly constant on the grounds, was very much greater during 1916. The marketed value of the product in the year 1915 was the greatest in the history of our Canadian fisheries, reaching a total of $35,860,708, which exceeded the total for the prewar year of 1913, by $2,652,960, notwithstanding the fact that 1913 was a big-run year on the Fraser river. So far as the incomplete figures for the past season permit us to arrive at conclusions, it would appear that the record value of our fisheries in
1915	has been substantially exceeded in 1916.
Looking at the figures for some of the chief kinds, we find that the quantity of lobsters landed ' in 1916 was 2 per cent greater, and the value 21 per cent greater than in 1915. Compared with 1913, the increase in quantity is 10 per cent, and in value 11 per cent, the prices paid by the canneries in 1913 being somewhat higher than those paid in 1916. The quantity of cod, haddock, hake and pollock taken in
1916	was 7 per cent less than in 1915, but the value was 14 per cent greater. The slightly diminished landings of those fish were due partly to the fact that there were not so many Lunenburg vessels engaged in the bank fishery, and partly to a scarcity of bait during the best part of the inshore fishing season. Compared with 1913, however, the catch of 1916 was 24 per cent greater, while the value was greater by 52 per cent.
The quantity of herring and mackerel landed in 1916 was 25 per cent less than in 1915, and 32 per cent less than in 1913. The value, however, did not fall to the same extent, as prices were from 50 per cent to 100 per cent above normal. The total catch of halibut in 1916 fell below that in 1915 by 8 per cent, but there was an increase in value. Compared with 191-3, the catch of 1916 was 13 per cent, and the value 60 per cent greater. In the year 1913, however, American vessels had not begun to land their catches at Prince Rupert.
The sardine fishery resulted in a decrease of 11 per cent in quantity, but an increase of 37 per cent in value when compared with 1915. Comparing the past season's catch with that of 1913, we find an increase of 100 per cent in quantity and 167 per cent in value. The movements of these small fish like the movements of all the herring kind, are uncertain, and as they are captured al-

most entirely by fixed appliances, the fluctuation in the quantity taken from year to year is consequently considerable. The value has increased much in keeping with that of other canned products since the outbreak of war.
The smelt fishery, owing to lack of ice. on the rivers, was not so productive as usual, the falling off in 1916, compared with 1915, was 6 per cent in quantity, but there was an increase of 22 per cent in value. Compared with 1913, the catch of 1916 was 14 per cent less, while the value was 16 per cent greater.
Complete returns of men and material employed in the fisheries during 1916 are not yet at hand, but a comparison of the number of fishing bounty claims paid in the past season with the number paid in the preceding year indicates that fewer vessels, fewer boats and fewer men were engaged in the fisheries of the Atlantic coast. In 1915 bounty was paid on 13,926 boats and to 24,670 boat fishermen. In the past year the numbers were 12,350 boats and 21,700 boat fishermen, with a few late claims likely to come yet. In 1915 bounty was paid to 6,107 vessel fishermen in vessels aggregating 23,638 tons. In the past year there were 5,450 vessel fishermen in vessels aggregating 20,150 tons to whom bounty was paid, with a few late claims also likely to come in.
Our boat fishermen and those who fish in inshore waters now find the motor-boat indispensable to the success of their operations. It gets speedily to and from the fishing grounds quite independently of winds, tides, and, in a great measure, weather conditions. Also, it permits operations over a greater range of fishing grounds than was possible with the old sail boat. We do not know exactly how many motor-boats were used in the fisheries of 1916, but the figures for 1915, and the precedifig four years, are illustrative of the rapid advance made in the use of such craft. In 1911 there were 5,580 motor fishing boats in the whole of Canada; in 1912, 5,911; in 1913, 8,700; in 1914, 9,302, and in 1915, 11,097.
Improvements are constantly taking place in the handling and manufacturing of cured fish of all kinds. The proportion of the inshore catch of cod, hake, etc., that is dried is annually growing less, while that used fresh and cut for the boneless trade is increasing and bringing enhanced values. In the pickled fish trade, through the stimulus of the Fish Inspection Act, increased attention is being given to the production of better packages and to improving the grade and quality of the pack. We are now using

in the salt mackerel trade an iron-hooped hard wood barrel superior to that used in any other country. Manufacturers of the finnan ihaddie, which is the mainstay of the smoked fish business, have within the last four or five years greatly improved its palatableness by realizing that too much salt and smoke applied to a fish that is really intended for almost immediate use are apt to curtail its consumption.
Looking at it all over, the production of our fisheries in 1916 is very gratifying. This gratification is mingled, with regret, however, because of the reported loss of 23 fish-erment while pursuing their calling on various parts of our coasts. In view of the preparations that aTe being made for. the coming season, and of the fact that this is the big run year for salmon on the Fraser river, we may look upon it as quite within the range of the probabilities that the value of the output in 1917 will reach the $40,000,000 mark.

The past season is the second in which inspection has taken place. There were in all 7,213 barrels of herring, alewives and mackerel presented for the brand. Of that number 2,688 were refused the brand, because of either poor quality of fish, bad grading or inferior barrels. In the previous year, 1,328 barrels were presented for the brand, of which 117 were refused. The number presented for the brand and the number refused the brand by districts were as follows:
In the district of H. H. Mann, Cape Breton Island, 305 barrels were presented, of which 31 were refused owing to poor packages. In the district of R. Gray, Halifax, Guysboro, and Antigonish counties, N.8., 1,493 barrels were presented, of which 575 wore refused, because of too light salting and bad grading. In the district of A. R. Hilts, Lunenburg county westward and round to Kings county, N.S., 1,744 barrels were presented, of which 238 were refused for bad grading. It was ultimately discovered that 400 barrels of this lot had deteriorated in quality and after a re-examination the brand was removed before final shipment. In the district of T. Doyle, Magdalen Islands, Prince Edward Island, and part of the Gulf shore of Nova Scotia, 91 barrels were presented, of which 62 were refused because of poor quality and bad grading. This officer devoted much time at the Magdalen Islands endeavouring by practical demonstration to improve the fishermen's methods of splitting, cleaning and
[Mr. Hazen-J
curing their mackerel, and while improvement undoubtedly resulted, he found that the fish generally were not cured entirely up to the standard required for the brand. In the district of C. Hubbard, Restigouche county to Kent county, N.B., 1,817 barrels were presented and 31 refused, owing to inferior packages, and the poor quality of the fish.
In the district of A .0. H. Wilson, Charlotte, St. John, Albert and Westmorland counties, N.B., 1,763 barrels were presented, of which 1,720 were refused because of leaky barrels and the poor condition of the fish.

Only a few were accepted. They were in poor barrels. I understand that the difficulty is now being overcome and that next year fishermen will have no trouble, owing to the improved methods of the coopers in getting good barrels so that the fish can be properly preserved and can be branded, and so command higher prices. In the district of A. O. H. Wilson, Charlotte, St. John, Albert and Westmorland counties, N.B., 1,763 barrels were presented, of which 1,720 were refused because of leaky barrels and the poor condition of the fish. The brand was taken advantage of by 73 separate packers against 16 in the preceding year. In the course of the year, 67 merchants and packers, including a number of individual fishermen, applied for and received instruction in herring-curing in the Scotch style.
The summer and fall herring fishing last season was little better than a failure on the Atlantic coast, and as a result not more than 30 packers actually cured herring in the Scotch method. Of these, 22 presented their pack for inspection and the brand. Fifteen cooperages which produce barrels in considerable quantities, applied for and received instruction in Scotch barrel making. These were located as follows:- I in Ontario, 2 in New Brunswick, and 12 in Nova Scotia. A number of scattered individual coopers, who make a few barrels for split herring, were also visited, as they could be located, and instruction given them. Perfection in barrel-making has not yet been reached, but many of the coopers are now turning out a rbally good barrel.
It should be kept in mind that the amount or value of the work performed by the in-

specting officers, cannot be measured by the actual number of barrels presented to them for the brand, because inspection is not obligatory. Hon. gentlemen will remember, when the Bill was passed it was made permissive, it was at the option of those who were doing the packing as to whether they would have inspection or not. As the demand for almost any kind of fish is abnormal at present, it frequently happens that a packer, after benefiting by the visits and instruction of our officers, ships off his fish without waiting for the officer to return and brand them.
In addition to the instructions contained in the Act and its regulations, the department in the beginning of last year issued to the trade pamphlets of special instructions in barrel-making and curing in the Scotch method. Prior to the fishing season and during its progress, each officer visited packers, barrel-makers and dealers within his district and kept before them the merits of the inspection system and endeavoured to persuade packers to cure their fish in accordance with the requirements of the Act. Instructional pamphlets will again be distributed to coopers and packers for their guidance this year, while practical demonstrations in barrel-making and curing will be continued.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: HERRING PISHING OPERATIONS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
In the course of the past summer, the department fitted out one of its steamers with herring drift-nets, for the purpose of endeavouring to locate the herring schools off shore in the Atlantic, and to catch them at a time when the fish are in the best condition for curing for the best markets. It is difficult for one boat to accomplish much in the course of one short herring season. A considerable amount of success was met with, however, notwithstanding a general failure in the herring fishery, and much valuable information secured concerning the size and quality of fish on the different grounds worked over. The boat began operations about the middle of May, and continued till the latter part of August. Fishing grounds extending from off Victoria county in Cape Breton to those off Shelburne county in Nova Scotia, were operated on. In all, 388 barrels of herring, and 5,622 barrels of mackerel were secured. June and July were the best months. Herring were scarce in August, and dogfish very plentiful. A detailed report of the quantity and quality of fish taken on the various fishing grounds has been printed and distribut-
 ,
ed to' those in the trade who are concerned in the business.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: DAILY BAIT REPORTS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
For the purpose of assisting masters of fishing vessels to locate bait supplies during the cod fishing season, the department operates a system whereby definite information concerning bait along certain stretches of the Atlantic seaboard is collected by the local fishery officers and despatched daily, by telegram, to certain important sea ports, and there posted up. The number of ports selected as receiving stations is necessarily limited, in the interest of economy, but through the courtesy of the Halifax daily papers, in which the telegrams are published each day, the smaller fishing centres also derive the benefit of direct advice as to available supplies of bait. Copies of all telegrams received at the receiving stations are mailed to the department at the end of each week, by which means the work is closely followed and checked. During the spring of the past year, ninety telegrams were sent from the Magdalen islands, Souris, P.E.I., and Queensport, N.S., to Canso, Halifax, Lunenburg and Biverport, N.S. During July and August, 195 telegrams were sent from Little Bras d'Or, L'Ardoise, Canso and Musquodoboit Harbour, N.S., to North Sydney, Canso, Halifax, Lunenburg and Shelburne, N.S.; also from Lockeport, N.S., to Canso and Halifax, N.S.; from Shag Harbour to Halifax, Shelburne and Lockeport, N.S. From the beginning of September to the end of November, 66 telegrams were sent from Campobello, N.B., covering information from the counties of Charlotte and St. John, N.B., to Digby, Yarmouth, Pubnico and Clark's Harbour, N.S. The information contained in the telegrams was of much benefit to line fishermen who were in search of bait, by directing them to where supplies were available, and to net fishermen who had bait to sell by bringing purchasers to them.
As will be seen from the foregoing, considerable is being, done to educate the fishermen and encourage them in the adoption of better methods, but some definite and comprehensive system of technical education all along the lines connected with their work is needed, and the matter is receiving attention, in order that everything may be in readiness to begin work as soon as possible after the return of peaceful days. Fishermen have not had sufficient pride in their calling, and too often their sons have been encouraged to

take up other vocations. There is consequently a shortage of skilled fishermen, and just at a time when they are urgently needed. When the war is over, it would be a good thing if skilled fishermen from desirable European countries wishing to immigrate would come to Canada. They would find splendid opportunities here, and I think it will be admitted that we need them for the proper development of this industry, which offers employment to so many people.	*
This afternoon the hon. member for Digfby (Mr. Jameson), who moved a resolution that it was desirable that the Department of Fisheries should he established under the control pi a separate minister who would devote his entire attention to the encouragement and development of the fisheries alone, said that, in his opinion, the increase in the growth of our fisheries had not been satisfactory. If I recollect correctly, he told the Hpuse that $75,000,000 was the value of the fisheries in the United States, while the value of the fisheries in Canada last year was $35,000,000. I think my hon. friend ought to bear in mind that the conditions in the two countries are not similar. *I do not think that the comparison which my hon. friend makes is one that justifies or bears out his contention. We must remember that the United States to-day is a nation of about 100,000,000 people, that the American fishermen have a market for their fish right at their very doors, that the industry there has been much longer established than in this country, and that there are a great many more men engaged in it than are engaged in fishing in' Canada, If he compares our population of less than
8,000,000 with the American population of nearly 100,000,000, he will see that our production of $35,000,000 worth, which will be increased this year to $40,000,000 worth, is not an unfavourable one for Canada. There is no doubt, as my hon. friend stated, that Canada's fishing grounds are the most extensive in the world. We have on the Atlantic coast about 5,000 miles of sea coast, running from the Ste. Croix river around New Brunswick and Nova Scotia up the gulf of St. Lawrence. We have on the Pacific coast some 7,500 miles of sea coast, not counting indentations and many of the hays, and we have also in Ontario and in the (western provinces, very extensive fresh water lakes in which many fish like white-fish, sturgeon, pickerel and others pf very considerable value are to he found. There is no doubt that as the development 129
of the country proceeds, as the number of our fishermen increases £tnd as a greater market for their product becomes available, there will be a much larger production of fish than there has been in years past. In making that assertion, may I point out that from the year 1886 until a few years ago, little or no progress was made in the Atlantic fisheries. My hon. friend is disposed to attribute this circumstance to lack of proper attention by the department in charge. While it is true- that there was very little progress in the Atlantic fisheries during the time referred to, it is fair to beaT in mind that the conditions prevailing before 1886 were much more favourable to the Atlantic fisheries than the conditions, during many years following that date. From 1854 until a year before Confederation a reciprocity treaty had been effective under which fish and the products of the fisheries were admitted into the United States markets free of duty. In 1872 the Treaty of Washington was entered irto, which again gave the freedom of United States markets to our fishermen. This treaty remained effective until 1885, and its provisions were much more important to our fishermen at that time than they would be now. Again, the mackerel fishery was at its zenith during the years prior to 1886. The quantity of mackerel taken then was nearly three times as much as the. quantity taken now, the value being nearly double. Moreover, the general conditions in the country from 1886 onward for a number of years were not such as to afford much opportunity for the rapid development of out Atlantic fisheries. No doubt the pickled fishing industry could have been greatly developed under proper conditions, but it was a difficult matter to find capital ready for investment in that direction, and the competition of a well-established business from Europe had to be met and overcome. Under the Fish Inspection Act, applied three years ago, and which has been in operation two seasons, the necessary steps to develop this industry are now being taken.
My hon. friend points out that the original department was the Department of Marine and Fisheries. No doubt the work of that department has enormously developed since its inception a year or two after Confederation. A judge of the Supreme Court of Canada who was Minister of Marine and Fisheries from 1896 to 1902 said the other day that the department, from what he saw of it, must ha.ve ten

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
times as much work to do now as it had during his time. Other work has since been added to the department.. Some years ago the work of the St. Lawrence ship channel was administered by the Department of Public Works, but when Mr. Prefontaine was Minister of Marine and Fisheries that work was transferred to that Department. Then,	it	was provided by	theterms	of	the	Naval Act	that	the
Minister of Marine and Fisheries should be the Minister of Naval Affairs. I assume it was thought at the time that there would not be very much work in the Department of Naval Affairs. That was the case for a time, and that wae the reason why we [DOT]divided the department. When I came into the department I found the Marine and Fisheries Branch very much overburdened with work, while the Naval Service Branch had not nearly so much to do. For the purpose, therefore, of equalizing the work, the administration of matters pertaining to the Fisheries was handed over to the Department of Naval Service. The Fisheries Department administers the Fisheries Protection fleet and the Fisheries Patrol fleet, both of which services logically come under the Department, of Naval Service. There is no. doubt that the work has enormously extended. While that is the case, I think the hon. member for Digby jumped at too hasty a conclusion when he intimated that the work of the Fisheries Department was being neglected and had been neglected ever since the department was formed. He asserts that during all these years, even when the work of the department was not so extensive, proper and adequate attention was not given to the development of our fisheries. I shall not argue that much more cannot be done than has been done, but the fisheries officers of the department-I know them intimately-are very capable men indeed. Mr. Found is wonderfully well informed with regard to fishery matters, is a most energetic official and active in the discharge of the duties of his position. The same may be said of Professor Prince, a scientific man connected with the Fisheries Department, as well as the other fishery officers.
During the past five years great attention has been given to the development of our fisheries with the result that many waters that were being rapidly depleted a few years ago, have been replenished with fish. There has been also an increase in the salmon fisheries of the Atlantic coast, and in many other directions considerable de-
TMr. Hazen.J
velopment has been attained. This is true in respect of all branches of the fisheries, with the exception of the oyster industry, which, unfortunately, for quite a number of years showed a steady diminution. I am glad to say, however, that under arrangements made between the Federal and the Provincial Governments, barren bottoms are being leased for replanting, and the chances are that along the coast of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, as has been the case in United States, a great development of that industry will take place, with great benefit to the oyster fishermen and to those who have been enterprising enough to put their money into the work of development which is now going on.
I am not prepared to discuss whether or not there should be another department to take charge of the fisheries. My hon. friend has suggested that the reason why Newfoundland does not come into the union is because they fear that sufficient attention will not be paid to their fisheries, I thin^ that is the first time that reason has been suggested; I always understood that other reasons induced a great many of the people of Newfoundland not to look favourably upon the idea of a confederation with the other provinces of British North America. I sincerely hope that that idea is disappearing, because I think it would be a splendid thing for Newfoundland, for Canada and for the Empire, if Newfoundland should eventually come into the union, situated as it is at the mouth of the St. Lawrence and at the very entrance to the heart of Canada. I do not tbiink my hon. friend can find the slightest justification for the argument that he has put forward in this respect. It may be that fishery matters in Canada can be treated with greater energy. One of the difficulties encountered at present is that a great, many men have gone away to fight and there are not as many men available to engage in the industry as there were some years ago. At present there is a market for all the Canadian fish that can be produced. The home market is increasing. People at points distant from the sea-board, owing to the campaign of education that has been taking place, are beginning to appreciate in greater degree the value of fish as a food. In view of the high price of meat of all kinds, fish will doubtless be sought more than it has been in the past. Moreover, our fish are being sold in increasing quantities in the American markets, and large quantities of Canadian fish are being sent over to Great Britain not only for our

soldiers, but for the purpose of feeding the civil population as well. The reason for that is that in Great Britain the condition of affairs is such that many of the trawlers in the North sea have been driven off the waters, some having been torpedoed, others havings been taken over by the Admiralty. When I was in Great Britain a few weeks ago, I was talking to a gentleman in Grimsby, one of the largest ' fishing centres in that country, and he told me that from the port where he lived there had usually, in normal times, been 36 trawlers sailing out into the North sea, but that at the present time there were only five trawlers engaged in the fishing business. As a result, there is not the same supply of fish from home -waters or from water contiguous to Great Britain for sale in the different markets, and there is a market there for Canadian fish, for the use not only of our soldiers but of the civil population as well. I asked that gentleman whether it was likely that the trade in frozen fish in Great Britain would be permanent, and his idea was that it would not; that after the war, when the fishing industry in Great Britain again assumed its normal condition, when the trawlers were all in commission again, bringing in fish daily for distribution throughout the country, it would be unnecessary for the British to have frozen fish brought from Canada, as they would have an ample supply for themselves. I think it is perfectly clear that the consumption of fish in Canada must and will develop, and year by year people are realizing, through instrumentalities such as the Toronto Exhibition, the distribution of literature, the discussion of this matter in Parliament, the discussion that goes on in the press from time to time, the value of fish as a food. When conditions again become normal, no doubt there will be an enormous development of our fisheries on our sea coasts and on our lakes. It is most gratifying to know that in lake Winnipeg and in our Ontario lakes where the fish were depleted years ago, the result of the fish breeding hatcheries has been that more fish are to be found in those lakes to-day than during the past generation.
My hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) has done good service in bringing this matter to the attention to the House. As he said, it is not often we have a discussion in this Parliament on an economic question. We can discuss this matter without any prejudice and without any idea of gaining any party
129i
advantage, because we are all only too anxious to develop the great resources of [DOT]the country, to make them as valuable to our people as possible and to preserve them as far as we can for the use of future generations.
After the war there will possibly have to be a very general change in .regard to the departments of Government, and probably this House will have to consider the desirability of having a naval department standing iby itself with a separate minister entirely apart from the minister who administers the Department of Fisheries. -We may find it necessary to do as has been done in Australia, where the system has been adopted of having a defence minister, who administers both the War Department and the Naval Department. To-day my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) stated that he has received letters suggesting that a separate Department of Mines ought to 'be created under a minister, for the purpose of developing the mining industry of the country. These suggestions are all, of course, subject to consideration, and I for one am not prepared to say that they do not carry weight, but at the same time we must bear in mind that for a country with a population of less than
8,000,000 we have a large Government as it is; we have some 17 or 18 ministers and more than that number of departments because some ministers preside over, more than one department. The whole question is one that cannot be determined simply on a resolution of this character dealing with one department of the Government; it will have to be dealt with from a more general standpoint when the war is over.
So far as my department is concerned, as my hon. friend has pointed out to-day, it is finding a great deal of work to do and has more subjects to deal with than any other department of Government. A great deal of additional work has been thrown on our shoulders, not only in the Naval Department, but in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, as a con-
9 p.m. sequence of conditions that have been created by the war. I would like to pay this tribute to the men and women in my department with whom I am working every day: for I have always found them anxious, ready and willing to undertake that extra work, and cheerfully to do what they can, under the abnormal circumstances that exist, to keep the work of the department up to the mark and, as far as possible, promptly to deal -with all questions that come befbre the

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
department. As minister of the department, I cannot, as my hon. friend says, give my entire attention to the fisheries or to any one branch of the department. Not only has a minister the duties of his department to attend to, but he has to attend to his work in Parliament; he has the affairs of his constituents to attend to-and that is not a small work when he repre-, sents a large constituency-and he has also to give time to certain political questions that have to be considered from time to time. Canadian ministers do what ministers do in England: The departments have permanent heads who are men of capacity and ability, and the different branches of the departments are presided over by men of ability. The different matters that come up for consideration have to be thought out by the permanent heads of the department, and then those matters are submitted to , the [DOT] minister who has to use his very best judgment in coming to a conclusion according to the facts presented to him. No minister can spend his time in digging up those facts for himself or in classifying them; he has to depend on the judgment of others, and in many cases men in this country and in every other country are called upon to preside over departments concerning the work of which they have had no previous knowledge. That is so in Great Britain. The Earl of Derby is called to be Minister of War; Sir-Edward Carson, a lawyer, is made First Lord of the Admiralty, and Mr. Bonar Law, a man who in his earlier days was engaged in the iron business, becomes Chancellor of the Exchequer. The same thing prevails in this country. You cannot have for Postmaster General a man who has always been a postmaster and who has had a knowledge of postal affairs, and all a minister can do is to do as a judge does, to bring his intelligence to bear upon the different questions with which he has to deal, obtaining from those who are acquainted with the work of the department, the best knowledge they can lay before him and obtaining the best views that he can get, and then to make up his mind. Other men might possibly be able to do more work than I can perform; but there is a limit to what any man can do, and I know that in my department at the present time, so -far as my officials are concerned and so far as I myself am concerned, every minute of our time is occupied. When conditions become more normal, a distribution may be made that will be mqre in the public interim Mr. Hazen.]
est; but T do not wish to admit for one moment that my predecessors in- office neglected the interest of the fisheries, and, so far as I am concerned, I desire to say that every attention that is (possible under existing circumstances has been given to the development of the fisheries, and if I -can rely on the judgment of my fishery officials more work of development has taken place during the past four or five years than in many years previously.

subtopic: DAILY BAIT REPORTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the minister on his new departure. I am sure that his address has been listened to with a great deal of interest by members on both sides of the House. It has'often occurred to me that it would be a good thing that when the Minister of Marine and Fisheries asks for his Estimates fpr the year, he should make a statement of the work of the past year and the policy that the department intends to pursue for the year to come. The minister has adopted that suggestion. While we listened with interest, as we always d-o, to his smooth and persuasive speech some of us were not a little disappointed that he has not been able to work out a more progressive policy. I sympathize with the attitude taken by my bon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) that the Department of (Marine andi .Fisheries, and especially the Fisheries Branch has not been conducted vigorously in the past, and has not done the work that the country expected it to do. My hon. friend from Digby intimated that the colony of Newfoundland had kept out of the Union for fear their fisheries would be neglected if they joined this Dominion. I do not know whether that is the case or not, but I cannot help feeling that the fishing interests of the province from which I come would have been in much better shape than they are in to-day if they remained undeT local control. Other industries in the province of Nova Scotia have made splendid progress. We have been able to develop a great coal mining industry, a very important fruit industry, as well as a great agricultural industry. All of these are under the control of a vigorous local Administration. On the other hand the fishing industry, which is really one of the most important in our province, has been marking time for practically half a century. In the last report of the 'Marine and Fisheries Department you will find that there has been no increase during the last 30 years in the value of the fish caught. But that

does not tell the whole story. During that period there was really a decrease in the quantity of fish caught, but on account of the higher price the total value of the catch kept up to the level of thirty years ago. Now that is not a very good Tecord, especially for the provinces of Nova Scotia which is the great fishing province of eastern Canada. Whatever progress has been made has been made largely in the province of British Columbia, where the salmon and halibut industry have been developed. The fact that the total value of the fisheries of Canada show an increase is due to the progress that has been made in British Columbia, and not because of any proigress in the Maritime Provinces or in Quebec. I attribute the development of the industry on the Pacific coast partly to the fact that the railway express companies have dealt with the transportation question in a vigorous manner. There the Dominion Express Company as a means of transportation has been very successful; but our experience has been different in eastern Canada. The remedy that my hon. friend from Digby suggests is to appoint a Minister of Fisheries. I do not know whether that will be of any great value. I think it would be quite suffiicent if a little more life could be infused into the present minister. If he would only show a little more vigour and enthusiasm, introduce necessary reforms in the department, I think we could, get along very well with one minister. But the minister must give his officials a lead. I do not object to the proposal of my hon. friend from Digby, but I do not think it is the best remedy. The situation requires something more, and I think it could be met by the present minister if he would only show more energy and conduct the department on business principles.
My hon. friend has referred to the fact that last year the Marine and Fisheries Committee held a number of meetings and carefully investigated the fisheries of this country, but, as my hon. friend from Digby pointed out, we were not honoured with a visit from the minister during the whole session. The committee in their report made certain recommendations, which the minister has gone over very carefully tonight, indicating to what extent they have been carried out. He failed, however, to show that anything substantial has been done. An attempt was made to do something in the way of inspection. A man was sent to Mulgrave we are told for two or three months to look after shipments
from that point- The minister withdrew the man and never expects to send him back again. That was a very abortive attempt in the direction of inspecting shipments. Everybody knows that fish is the most per- ^ ishable article on the market. No other article begins to decay so quickly, and it is therefore of the utmost importance to have the best transportation facilities. There should be a cold storage at the terminals, and quick transport by refrigerator cars; the fish should be got to the market in good condition and with as little delay as possible. Without these facilities the fishing industry cannot be developed. The minister's attempt at inspection was so ridiculous that nobody will regard it as a final attempt. We shall not be satisfied until something more is done.
I need not point out to the House that the fishing industry is capable of very great development. My hon. friend from Digby pointed out that for the capital invested, no* Canadian industry gives such a large return. The industry has a capital [DOT]invested'.' of about $25,000,000, which includes wharves,, warehouses, and all appliances on land as; well as the boats, vessels, and nets that are used on the sea, and that investment of $25,000,000 brings in a yearly return at present of $35,000,000. I do not think that can be said of any other Canadian industry. There is no reason why that $35,000,000 could not be enormously increased, doubled or trebled, in fact, with proper facilities. We have assisted many other industries in this country by bonuses. We have spent from $16,000,000 to $20,000,000 in bonusing the steel industry, and as a result a great industry has been built up in this country which otherwise we probably should not have had. The fishermen are self reliant and they are not asking for anything of that kind so far as I know. What they are asking for is a chance to carry on their business; they want the facilities for developing the industry, not a cash bonus.
The greatest question of all is transportation. We cannot develop the fishing industry unless we can improve transportation from the place where the fish is caught to the market My own constituency affords a very good illustration of that fact. About twenty years ago the town of Canso in my constituency was carrying on a fishing business in the old-fashioned way. They had no proper means of sending fresh fish to market because at that time there was no daily boat connecting the town of Canso with the Intercolonial at Mulgrave. The;

X would strongly recommend that the incoming Executive Committee spare no effort to secure the improved facilities and proper service from the various transportation companies handling our products, from which they derive large revenues. I suggest that the assistance of the Naval Service Department of our Federal Government he again enlisted with this object in view.
It is, therefore, the opinion of the president of the Fisheries' Association that our methods of transportation between the Maritime Provinces and Montreal are obsolete and as a result we have not been able, with these methods, to build up anything approaching a great fishing industry. Still the minister seems to be quite satisfied with these methods. I do not know whether we can do anything more to convince him or not, but in looking over the list of recommendations made by the special committee of this House on fisheries, I cannot find that very much has been done. The first of the recommendations which was made is one in regard to inspection. An abortive attempt was made at Mulgrave to do something in the way of inspecting shipments, but my hon. friend seems to have abandoned the idea o.f doing anything more. The second is:-
That the express facilities be so improved as to ensure daily transportation of sea foods from the east by means of the chilled car service.
Nothing has been done in the direction of improving the express service from the East.
3.	That the refrigerator car service for the transportation of sea foods be so improved as to render it available on express trains.
That has nqt been done.
4.	That the consolidation of shipments for different points in the express refrigerator car, on the basis of carload express rates, to the farthest point, and the opening of ear in transit to set down fish at different centres en route, would materially aid prompt and economical distribution of sea foods.
I have heard it questioned whether that is a practical proposal or not, hut at all events there has been apparently no investigation and no attempt to carry it out. The next is<-
That a carload lot express rate, substantially lower than the L.C.L. rate should be fixed on sea goods from the east.
That has not been done. Recommendation No. 6 has been carried out, but No. 6 simply recommends that the old quantity be restored. It is:-
That the minimum freight carload quantity, on the Government Railway be reduced from the new scale of 24,000 pounds to the former scale of 20,000 pounds.

That was the proposal and that has been done. I never saw any good reason for increasing the minimum carload quantity and there was so much opposition to the increase that my hon. friend apparently secured the consent of the railway department to the proposed reduction. For this we must give him credit.
8. That an exclusive express service operated by the Government be inaugurated on the Intercolonial Railway and Prince Edtward Island sections of the Government railways, as a preliminary to any general scheme for the nationalization of express business in Canada.
My hon. friend has made no reference at all to any attempt to deal with this important recommendation.
I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that after this committee had devoted most of a month to investigating this matter to the best of their ability and had brought in their recommendations, they were unanimously adopted iby the House of Commons. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should have attempted immediately or as soon as possible to carry them out. Most of them are very practical suggestions but no attempt has been made to comply with them and no satisfactory explanation has been given to show why they have not been complied with.
I might refer to the apparent disregard of the department of the interests of fishermen on the question of salt. This question arose during the present season. It became known last winter that the freight rates were so high that it would be difficult for the merchants on the coast to secure salt enough to carry on the fishing trade and as early as February last correspondence was opened with the Department of Trade and Commerce asking the Government to do something in the way of providing tonnage to carry salt across the Atlantic so that the fishing industry could be carried on. The fact is that little has been done, and it transpires now from evidence that has been placed! before the House by the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that transport ships have been coming across the Atlantic empty in connection with the work of the Admiralty and that some of these ships have been carrying mud ballast from the other side and that it has been costing $1.25 a ton to discharge this ballast out in Bedford Basin. With proper foresight these ships could have come over with salt instead of mud and there would have been plenty of salt available to carry on the fishing industry.
If the minister had 'been alive to the interests of the fishermen he would not have

allowed a circumstance like that to have taken place but he would have approached the Admiralty and seen that tonnage was secured in order that the fishing industry might have a sufficient supply of salt for the season.
I hope that, even if we do not succeed in getting a Minister of Fisheries alone, we may be able to get some kind of progressive policy from the department as at present organized. The minister could do a great deal that he has not done. He has, I believe, capable and energetic officials, some of whom are as good men as he could find anywhere but these officials want a lead from himself. The minister is the man to whom we have to go with ,dur complaints and criticisms, and he is the man who is responsible for the administration of his department, and not his officials. I trust he will bestir himself and take steps to put into practice the recommendations .of the Fisheries Committee looking towards the development of this important industry. A programme has been outlines by the committee which contains, I think, the principal things that are required at the present time. It is reshits that we want, and want them now; we do not want to wait for them too long. My hon. friend has been in office for six years, and I am sorry to say there is really not very much that he can show of a progressive nature that he has attempted or accomplished. I am not opposed to the proposed addition to the Cabinet but I am not inclined to swap horses now when we are crossing the stream, I would rather have some results from the present minister and I hope that, after the discussion to-night in which it has been again drawn to his attention that the transportation facilities are in such a backward state, he will endeavour to do something to have them improved.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton) :
subtopic: DAILY BAIT REPORTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been greatly interested in the addresses of the hon. member who introduced this resolution (Mr. Jameson) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The subject has been very fully dealt with by the minister and by the hon. member for 'Guysfoorough. It is not a new subject to this House, and I shall not go over grounds that have been traversed in the years that are gone toy. I wish to say a few words on this great subject of fisheries, and as a preliminary I would say that the fishing industry and the fish products of Nova Scotia have never had a fair show in this country, have
never been fairly brought to the notice of the consuming people of Canada beyond the province itself. There is a large market for fish in the various cities of Quebec and Ontario, but we have not been in a position to put that excellent product in its inviting condition and with its proper tasting qualities before the people, as it has been injured in transit as a rule, and what is a most palatable and , excellent aiticle when it leaves Nova Scotia' becomes stale and distasteful and uninviting before it reaches the table of the consumer in the central provinces. To overcome these difficulties should be our principal object. It is, of course, interesting and encouraging to be able to say that we have the fish in abundance. When people launch upon any enterprise, it is well to be sure that they have in abundance the article with which they propose to deal. Sometimes men launch their capital upon mining speculations only to find after they have spent it that the mineral which they expect to find is not in their property. We are far past that stage, so far as the fisheries of Nova Scotia and all of Canada are concerned. The fish are there in abundance and of the very best quality. It so happens that I represent a section of the province .of Nova Scotia which is the home of fisheries on a very large scale. So in discussing fisheries I might be accused of being local in my observations because I talk of matters in my own constituency; but I do not think that makes it any less important to talk about those things and to present them, because a very large section of the very cream of the fishing grounds of the province of Nova Scotia happens to be along the coast of the island of Cape Breton of which Cape Breton North and Victoria forms a part. As I have said, it is encouraging to be able to tell the minister and the Government that we have the fish. We have it in tons and millions of tons, and anything that we have caught of the fisheries in the province of Nova Scotia is but touching the fringe of an unlimited quantity that is available there. So much then for the quantity that is there. As the minister has pointed out, from the western coast of New Brunswick along the whole coast of that province, the province of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island and up to the frozen north is one continuous fishing ground of the richest and best quality. The fish is there, there is no question about that. The next thing, of course, is that the fish must be caught. Let me say to

the minister that it is useless to think of making a development or an advance along these lines without the expenditure of money. We must all take our share of responsibility for putting the money at the disposal of the department in order to find the facilities to catch the fish and place it on the market. I think that all Ministers of Marine and Fisheries in this country since Confederation have been a little too timid about the amounts of money they should have and could have expended in connection with the development of the fishing industry, and I hope that the present minister and future ministers will enlarge their ideas in that respect and spend more money. I may be asked, what are you going to spend the money for, what are you going to do with the money? And I may point out, as has already been pointed out, that while it is certainly not the duty of the Government to send out men in boats to catch the fish, it is the duty of the Government to make the building and harbouring of boats and the going to and from the fishing grounds as safe and convenient ae possible. These are things that must he done by public money, that cannot be done by the enterprise of the fishermen alone. In the county from which I come, along the north coast of Cape Breton, we have very extensive fishing grounds, but they are along a forbidding rugged rocky coast with very few harbours. The money that has been spent in the development of those harbours and in the building of breakwaters has resulted in substantial benefit to the fishing industry. Though there is yet much to be done, we have been able to use larger boats, go further out into the sea and obtain bigger catches. Millions of tons of fish have been carried away from the very doors of our fishermen by American vessels, taken to a foreign country and sold, the profits that should be made by ourselves going to foreigners. The minister must get money from the public coffers for the development of the harbours and the encouragement of our own fishermen as well as of those whom we can induce to come from Newfoundland to develop our fisheries if the conditions are at all favourable.
After the fish is caught, proper facilities must be available for getting it to market as speedily as possible. The centres of trade and of consumption must be put in touch with the places where the fish are to be obtained. The minister need not apologize for spending money for this pur-

pose. The fishing industry can never be developed at Canso, for instance, a great fishing centre, by the use of a single boat running from Canso to the Intercolonial terminus at Mulgrave. The only way of solving the difficulty is by extending the railway to those points. Every inch of the coast line of Cape Breton should have railway accommodation, because the whole coast abounds in fish, and the greatest discouragement to the fishermen is the lack of transportation. The development of the harbours in the northern part of Victoria county has brought about good results. Two large American concerns have been doing business in that part of the country since the opening of the harbour of In-gonish, as a result of the appropriation of moneys voted by the late Administration. In getting these moneys for the development of harbours and breakwaters, I was regarded by many hon. gentlemen as spending money for the purpose of getting votes. I am sorry to say that that is the manner in which many members of this House view the expenditure of moneys for the opening of harbours' and the building of breakwaters to serve the needs of our fishermen. But, as I say, one of the results of the opening of the harbour of Ingonish has been the activity of these great concerns, the Gorten-Pew Company of Boston and the Thompson Company which have amalgamated, and the firm of Collis, Jones and Whitman. They handle hundreds of tons of fish every year, paying for them readily, saving a great deal of labour and enabling the people with whom they deal to obtain the fish in better condition than they could otherwise secure it. The provision of proper facilities for the catching and the marketing of fish cannot be made without an expenditure of money and a more active interest in the matter on the part of the minister. The Railway Depart-men have dealt with the transportation of fish as they would with passengers who had smallpox; the fewer they had and the quicker they got rid of them, the better they liked it. I fear that the minister regards all this discussion and the time which it takes up as a nuisance, and something that he would be glad to be rid of. But the only way to get rid of it is to make proper provision for the development of the fisheries, one of the most magnificent industries of Canada.
Last year and several years before, I asked the minister to make provision for bait along the coast. In the small colony of Newfoundland the Government provide steamboats with cold storage facilities that

carry an ample supply of bait for the use of the fishermen. No doubt, headquarters are provided which supply the steamers with bait from time to time. We have nothing of that kind. Surely we can do what the Government of Newfoundland, a country with a small population, can do. In the county from which I come, at certain seasons of the year when fish are practically running in on the shore in tons, the fishermen have no bait, and they suffer to that extent. Money devoted to development along the lines which I suggest would be well and profitably spent. Places should be established along the coast of Cape Breton and elsewhere in the province of Nova Scotia where bait could be obtained at any time by the fishermen, It is of no use to say that the fishermen themselves should establish these places; they have not done it in the past, and they will not do it now. If the minister, then, will take some steps to make it easy for the fishermen to catch the fish; if he will provide facilities for bringing that fish to market and take such other steps as I have suggested, he will be doing a great service to the people and will justify the expense of the department over which he presides.

I have listened with much interest to the remarks made by the minister with regard to the fisheries of Canada during the last year. I regret that what to my mind was the most important recommendation made by the Committee on Marine and Fisheries last year was passed over by the minister with this remark, that it was found that the recommendation was not required because the fish arrived at destination packed in ice, and in good condition. That remark may' be true in the months of April, May and June, but from my experience I can say that during the hot months of July and August fish do not arrive at destination properly preserved in ice, and that if compartments of the car were set aside and ice chambers used, the fish would arrive in much better condition. But that is really not the important part of the recommendation. It was clearly brought out before that committee that deterioration was very much greater in the winter season than in the summer season, and that matter was entirely passed over by the minister. On a previous occasion I have stated in the House that I can send a carload of fish to London, England, and it will arrive there in good order, whereas if I send a box of fish from my town to the city of Montreal during the winter season, I cannot expect it to arrive at Montreal in good condition. Why? Because frozen fish are placed in heated cars, and when they come into contact with the heat of the car, the frost is drawn from the fish and you can never get them back into proper condition, and unless they are consumed immediately, they deteriorate very quickly. The recommendation to which I have referred is the most important part of the recommendation of the Marine and Fisheries committee; yet the minister tells the House to-night that that recommendation was found not to be required at all. The minister instanced the fact that they put an express car on the route once a week. If I am not corerct, the minister will kindly correct me. I do not remember that he mentioned the day in the week that this car was put on the route, but he said that it started from Mulgrave and picked up the freight from Halifax. I do -not wonder that the car was taken off; I claim it is quite impracticable to put a car on once a week and expect that to satisfy the needs of the trade or to enable the producer to place fish in the market from day to day as is required. The shipment of fresh fish by expressmustnot be provided ononly one given day in the week. It is true, I will admit, that perhaps Tuesday would be the best day of the week for the shipment of fish, but one car a week will not meet the requirements. Nothing else will
10 p.m. meet the requirements except a car north on each of the six days in the week, and that car provided 'with a compartment where ice and 6alt can be put in the chamber so that the car may be kept cool. That is more important in the winter season than in the summer season, and yet the minister never referred to the matfer at all.
Another thing that is most important for our fishing industry is markets, and to-day we have in a foreign market that is friendly to Canada a considerable demand for salted codfish, but the duty on these goods entering that country practically prohibits our using that market. I think therefore that the Department of Marine and Fisheries should suggest to that country that they might reduce the rate of duty or perhaps permit that commodity to enter free. Let me give an instance. At one time codfish went to the markets of France and word came back that those fish were subject to a duty of forty-five francs per hundred kilograms, or about four cents per pound. That is something that the Department of

Marine and Fisheries or the Department of Trade and Commerce might take up in the interest of the fishing community of this country, especially at this time when the fishermen of France are not able to frequent the waters of St. Pierre and Miquelon, and when we would not interfere with the French fishermen if we had access to their market at a reasonable rate. If the Department of Marine and Fisheries would take up that matter, they would be doing something to aid and foster the fishing industry.
The minister informed us that the recommendation regarding the 20,000 pound car was undertaken, but he did not tell us whether the rate per hundred pounds was increased thereby. It is all very well for the railways to reduce the minimum carload from 24,000 pounds to 20,000 pounds and to increase the rate per hundred pounds. The minister did not tell us that the matter worked out in that way.
Let me refer just for a moment to what the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) referred as something that would encourage the industry perhaps as much as anything the Government could do.
I am glad to see the Minister of Railways in his seat on this occasion, because the re-maiks I have to make apply more particularly to his department. I know of nothing that the Government could do that would assist the fishing industry more than to take over the branch lines that are feeders for the Intercolonial railway and operate them as they should be operated. That would be a great boon to the fishing industry. Let me illustrate what I mean. On, the Caraquet railway lour or five weeks ago some eight or ten boxes of frozen fish were sent by the Dominion Express from Ship-pigan to Montreal. That railway took about four days to carry the fish from Shippigan to Bathurst, a distance of lees than 100 miles. By the time the fish arrived in Montreal they had deteriorated and were practically of no value. The operation of that railway has caused the loss of a considerable amount of fish. Last March several carloads of frozen fish were sold to Montreal, Toronto; and American markets. The railway was blocked with snow at the time, but the shipper hoped that the line would soon be cleared and that he would be able to get a refrigerator car in which to ship the fish. Day after day passed and no oar came. At last the weather commenced to get warm, and then the fish could not foe marketed. The goods are still in the freezer because [Mr. Lo^grie.l
the railway could not place a car at the shipper's disposal. The Government could give no greater encouragement to the fishing industry than by seeing that the feeders to the trunk line are properly managed. I want to congratulate the Minister of Railways for assenting to the proposition that the Government railways should come under the Railway Commission; that would be a boon to the fishing industry. At present the branch lines are constructed undeT provincial charter, but I hope the Minister of Railways will soon announce that he is going to take over and operate the branch lines and feeders in the interests of the fishing industry and of the people in the territory which they serve.
