When the warm weather comes we cannot sell frozen fish in any market practically. There are exceptions to that; for example, in the United Kingdom, in the month of August, when their salmon fishing is over, they will use our frozen fish. There is quite a demand for our Atlantic sea salmon in England in the month of August, but, as a rule, you cannot market frozen fish where fresh fish are available, and therefore it Is in the interests of the industry that facilities should be provided for placing the goods on the market at the proper season.
I just wish to say a word or two regarding the lobster fishing industry. The present season is some three weeks late. Weather conditions on the Atlantic coast have been

such that the season that should have opened about the 5th of May did not open until about the 25th of May. The season properly opens on the 25th of April and packers get to work about the 5th of May. On account of the bad weather this season, which delayed them until the 20th of May, they will probably have a very short pack.
I have always been opposed to extending the season, but in the interests of increased production I think the minister might well consider extending the season this year, when the matter is brought before him in the regular way. I have frequently told the minister that after the packing season closes a considerable amount of pilfering goes on. I have pointed out that to him year after year, and he has always replied that his officers say that it is not going on. I want to repeat to-night that it is going on. Within the last few days, when I was home, I was ^old that these men get a few traps and hardly use them at all during the season, but keep them for pilfering after the season has closed, when the lobsters are more plentiful and can be caught at considerably less expense. If the minister cannot stop illegal fishing after the 1st of July then he ought to let everybody fish. Close fishing down for a month and then let everybody have the same chance. It is unfair to allow [DOT] these men to engage in illegal fishing all along the coast, and it seems to be increasing every year. A market is found for the goods if there is any demand for them, although I have no doubt that fnany exporters would prefer to have nothing to do with them. But once the goods are packed they find a market. I am not prepared to say just how that is done, but I told the minister privately last year how I thought, it could be done. If the minister will see that the close season for packing lobsters is observed, I think he may be able to maintain the industry, but if some men are to be allowed to pack while others cannot, I say let him change the season; let us all pack for two or three weeks in the fall. The minister ought to put it on a business basis, and give those who have a large amount of money invested the same chance as those who fish for lobsters out of season.
I do not know that I need take up the time of the House any longer. I have talked along these lines on former occasions, and have perhaps referred to-night to one or two matters that I did not mention before. But the field is a great one. The possibilities of our fisheries are vast, and it behooves us to take care of the industry^ It is true that the deep sea fisheries are
not so much in danger as the coast fisheries. There are now being introduced in the waters of the St. Lawrence steam trawlers. What effect that will have on the fisheries, of coursd, I do not pretend to foretell. We always have felt that it was dangerous to have the trawlers come within a certain distance of our coast. But they do it in the North Sea, and many of these vessels come from Gloucester and Boston on our own coast, and so I suppose it is only fair that the same should be allowed from Canadian ports. I know that the industry in that line has been increased and, I believe, successfully. One argument in favour of the trawling system is that the operator is sure of a catch, whereas if you go put with hand lines or trawling with hooks, there is great risk from the weather. This means that the supply thus secured is uneven; sometimes there is too great a supply of fish, and sometimes none at all. With the trawlers the market can be supplied more regularly. Perhaps it *is not out of place that they should be allowed.
Another industry that, I think, might possibly be developed to some extent, is the herring industry. If the minister would try to facilitate the drifting for herrings at certain. seasons of the year and in certain waters, the results would be beneficial. It is alleged that there is a small herring, fat and suitable for the market in the months of July and August. I am not informed on this subject myself, but I have understood that traps are allowed for herring all the summer season on the Prince Edward Island coast. The traps are put put in the spring and kept out until the fall, a nominal fee of $15 being charged. But in some sections there seems to be objection to these traps. I do not say that they should be allowed in the rivers, -but I do npt see why they should not be allowed in the outside coast. Certainly I cannot understand why there should be objection to them in other places, when they are allowed on the shpres of Prince Edward Island.
I was very glad to hear the minister's address, and I have taken the opportunity to mention a few points in that address to which I take exception. I hope the subject of express facilities will be taken charge of by the minister, and that ho will not say tp the House again that these facilities are not needed. I know from personal experience that the recommendation on this subject is the most important made by the Marine and Fisheries Committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the indulgence of the House for a moment while I offer one or two observations with respect to the subject under discussion. No doubt the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) presented the amendment which he has made to the motion that the House resolve itself into Committee of Supply for the purpose of calling the attention of Parliament to the necessity for some further, and more vigorous action, on the part of the Government towards the development of the fishing industry throughout Canada. The object of his amendment is one that is to be commended and anything that can be done, or any discussion that is called for by such action on his part that will result in more remunerative employment and wider markets for our fishermen ought to be commended and supported by the members on both sides of this House.

We well remember that in 1911 the issue upon which the election was decided was that of^ reciprocity. 'Commissioners representing this country negotiated an agreement with the Government of the United States which resulted in opening to the products of Canadian farmers the large and remunerative markets of the United States. While that agreement was defeated in the election of 1911, it is within the knowledge of this House that quite recently one part of the reciprocity arrangement was put into operation by Order in Council passed by this Government which opened the markets of the United States to the products of the Canadian farmers in the West. But, that market is still closed to the products of the Canadian fisheries. Having regard to the importance of opening the United States market at this particular . time to one great branch of- our industry,
I think it might quite logically follow that the Government should have taken some steps to have opened a free market in the United States for the fisheries as well. The reciprocity agreement provided for the free entry into the United States of the products of the farm and the products of the fisheries and it would thus have conferred a distinct benefit upon the fishermen of the Maritime Provinces.
There is another item which enters into the fishing industry and which also came in for favourable treatment in that agreement. I refer to the article of salt. One of the greatest hindrances to the successful prosecution of the fisheries of the Maritime Provinces during the present season is the difficulty the fishermen have in obtaining an adequate supply of salt. Owing to the want of tonnage it is extremely difficult to obtain salt from the markets which heretofore have supplied it to our fishermen. Under the reciprocity agreement salt was to have been admitted free to the fishermen of the Maritime Provinces but that agreement having been defeated, our fishermen are still under the necessity of paying a duty of 7i cents a hundred pounds upon all salt imported. No greater stimulus could be given our fishermen by the present Government than to take immediate steps to remove the duty on salt. A very serious situation confronts our fishermen. The price of salt has increased fourfold during the last three years and I do know that many fishing communities in Nova Scotia have decided to abandon the salt fishery tnis year owing to the extreme difficulty of obtaining the salt that they require in the prosecution of their industry.
There is another matter that was to have [DOT] been dealt with by the reciprocity agreement and that was the amendment of the regulation known as the. modus vivendi by removing the license fee which heretofore had been imposed upon American fishermen coming into our ports for the purpose of purchasing bait, taking on supplies or shipping their fish to their own markets.
A license fee of $1.50 per ton is exacted upon all American fishing vessels coming into our ports for the purpose which I have mentioned. The reciprocity agreement contained the following clause:
The Government of Canada agree? that, until otherwise determined by them, the licenses hitherto issued to United States fishing vessels under the provisions of Section 3 of Chapter 47 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, granting to such vessels certain privileges on the Atlantic coast of Canada, shall continue to be issued and that the fee to be paid to the Government of Canada for such license by the owner or commander of any such United States vessel shall hereafter be one dollar per annum.
A very large business developed along the coast of Nova Scotia previous to the imposition of this license fee in the supplying of bait to the American, fishing vessels and a large trade also was developed by the merchants along the coast in supplying these vessels and their crews. The imposition of this license fee has resulted in these vessels keeping away from our ports. When their outfit is exhausted, instead of coming to the ports of Nova Scotia to refit, in order to avoid the payment of the license fee, they return to their own ports and this large business which could be built up by our merchants on the shores of Nova Scotia is interfered with.
There is another consideration which is very important in respect to this matter. It is well known that the fishing fleet of the United States is largely commanded and manned by Nova Scotia fishermen. These men are obliged to leave their homes along the shores of Nova Scotia in midwinter or early spring and to go to the United States to take their positions as masters or crews of these fishing vessels. They come to the waters of the Maritime Provinces, particularly those of Nova Scotia to prosecute their industry but they are unable to visit their	homes for the
purpose of transacting any business or of renewing their supplies for the reason that they, are prohibited by this license fee. During recent years a very large proportion of the American fishing fleet is made up of what is known as auxiliary fishing boats. [DOT] This license fee under

the modus vivendi does not apply to fishing vessels of that class so that no share of that part of the fishing business, which has gone to the United States, and which has grown up enormously within the last 15 or 20 years, accrues to the advantage of the people of Nova Scotia.
The object of the resolution which the hon. member for Digby has introduced is to find some means of increasing the pio-duct of the fisheries of Canada. There is no better way in which we can enlarge the output of the fisheries than by seeking freer and larger markets. Whatever may be said to the contrary by hon. gentlemen opposite, the fact remains that to a great extent our best and largest market is that of the United States. The abrogation of the treaty of 1818 has been asked for time and again by hon. members sitting on this side of the House. That is still a very live question and I for my part cannot see how any advantage can possibly accrue to the fishing industry of Canada by preserving the terms of the treaty or by preserving the modification of the treaty as embodied in the terms of the modus vivendi. I stated a moment ago that American vessels are not permitted to enter our ports for the purpose of obtaining supplies or prosecuting the fishery to the advantage of the people of Nova Scotia. But a different condition of affairs exists on the coasts of British Columbia.
At Prince Rupert there is a large fishing industry which has been developed in recent years, and which is carried on largely by fishing vessels that come up from the port of Seattle. These fishermen are allowed to fish off the waters of British Columbia. They can come into Prince Rupert and ship their fish to the United States market without paying the license fee which prevents vessels coming into the ports of Nova Scotia. I cannot understand why that distinction is made, and why privileges are granted to the fishing industry of British Columbia that are denied to us in Nova Scotia. The fishing industry would be very largely increased in Nova Scotia if a change were made in these regulations and the license fee entirely cancelled and the right given to fishing vessels of all nations to come into our ports to buy supplies. There is a very large demand for fish now in the British markets owing to the curtailment of fishing operations in the North sea. I am informed that buyers from the British markets go over to the United States and contract for the purchase of large quantities of fish which are

caught by American vessels and taken to American seaports. We do not find that in the province of Nova Scotia we are sharing the advantage of this large expansion in the British consumption of fish from this side of the ocean as a result of the war. I am informed that the Department of Marine and Fisheries have been considering the question of the removal of this license fee under the modus vivendi with the authorities at Washington. I do not know whether or not that is correct. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries will no doubt be good enough to give any information to the House that he can possibly give at present, but I for one would be very glad to learn, in the interests of the fishing communities of Nova Scotia, that some step was being taken by the Government to abrogate the treaty of 1818, and to remove from the statute books the modus vivendi which prohibits American fishing vessels from coming into the ports of Nova Scotia. A very large trade would be developed in Nova Scotia through our merchants doing business at the seaports if they were permitted to supply freely to these fishermen all goods necessary for them in prosecuting their fishing voyages. Not only are our fishermen prohibited from getting a very large market for fresh fish by supplying these fishermen with 'bait, but our merchants are deprived of the opportunity of furnishing other supplies to vessels, such as rubber boots, clothing, oilskins and underwear. This prohibition results, as I said, in diverting the trade which should belong to the merchants of Nova Scotia to .the supply houses in Massa-chussetts, and at the same time it 'has a very deterrent effect upon the development of our fisheries in the Maritime Provinces.
Mr. ARTHUR B. OOPP (Westmorland): I rise to discuss this question, which is of great importance to the fisheries in my own particular locality. I do not rise for the purpose of supporting the motion of my hon. friend particularly, because I do not want to support it in either of the two cases in which it may have been offered to this House. If it was a new policy that was intended to be adopted by the hon. members opposite with regard to having a new portfolio in the Cabinet we on this side would have little to say in regard to such a policy. But if it is a matter of voting want of confidence in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries I would not want to subscribe to it unless the hon. gentleman coupled the whole Government with the motion. I

would not want him to single out my Mend from New Brunswick in a vote of want of confidence in that hon. gentleman. If it included the whole Government I might be induced, in some manner, to consider the matter at least more carefully.
The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) has brought to the attention of this House an important matter in regard to the fishing industry of our country. It has been discussed very largely by gentlemen on this side of the House in relation to both the deep sea fisheries and coast fisheries. I was rather surprised during the course of the discussion to-night when I picked up a report recently issued on lobster fishery conservation in Canada by Mr. A. P. Knight. As I am .particularly interested in that branch of the fishing industry, in which .a large number of fishermen are engaged ' on the shores of my constituency and of all New Brunswick as well as Nova Scotia, I was astounded
to	learn	that during'	the	last	nineteen	years	the lobster	fisheries	havedecreased	a little	over	100	per	cent.My	hon.	friends	opposite	speak of	the	increase in	the	value	of	the
fisheries. Is is very easy to have the value increase as the price goes up, but the quantity is decreasing all the time, according t,o this report, and while I realized that there had 'been a decrease in the lobster catch in Canada, I had no idea that it had decreased to such an alarming extent as it has. My hon. friend from Digby, in discussing this matter this evening, made the statement that there was a good deal of dry rot, or that the Government or the department had got into a rut and that it was time it was taken out of this rut and put on a more businesslike basis, and more attention given to the different matters put before the department. I do not know whether that is a correct expression, whether the department is in a rut pr what is the reason, but, during the two or three years that I have had the honour to .have a seat in this House, I have looked into fishery matters to seme extent and Tead the reports that have been made from time to time. I have read the reports made in regard to the fishing industry of this country back for years and years, and the recommendations that have been made. Things of that nature have been brought before the people, but it does seem to me for some reason or other, whoever may be to blame, whether it is the minister over the department or his officials under him or whether it was because there was no one who had the information or 130

I notice that some years ago, twenty years ago for all I know, the lobster hatcheries were established in this country, There had been hatcheries for different kinds of fish all over Canada, and the lobster hatchery was introduced. I know that in my county we looked forward with great anticipation of the lobster hatchery being a good investment, and we hoped that the lobster catch would be very largely increased because of the hatcheries. I see by this very latest report by Mr. Knight, who is apparently an authority on this question, that instead of the lobster hatchery having been a benefit it is a menace to the lobster industry, and he lays down the principle that the lobster hatchery must be done away with and some pther arrangement or scheme entered into. I have not been able to read the whole of this very interesting report and the tables set out in it. He says:
What is to be done? It is useless to look to the hatcheries as a means of replenishing our depleted waters. Rather are they agencies of destruction than of conservation.
That is a statement by one who has made a study of this matter very recently, and if that is so, surely we have lpst 'a great deal of time besides wasting a great deal of money in the effort to replenish our lobster fisheries. According to the report made by Mr. Knight, the lobster catch has been decreasing year by year, and if some steps are not taken tp prevent it, sooner or later the industry will disappear altogether.

In a report on the subject, the inspector of fisheries in that portion of the province, Mr. Morrison, says that the lobster industry, which had fallen off to an alarming extent during the previous two years, was showing signs of improvement. But while that is true with regard to lobsters ,^st yeaT, there has been, a falling off of $94,469 in the value of the herring catch. There has been a falling off also in the mackerel catch, and the smelt catch has shown a falling off of $122,000. Cod also has shown a decrease.
I wish to, -refer to a matter that is very dear to my heart, and that is the shad
fishery. I	do not think they	havethe shad	fishery	in other parts	ofCanada as	we	have it in	theprovince of	New	[DOT]Brunswick. A	fi Vyears ago	it was a valuable	industry along the St. John, Kennebeeasis, and Petiteodiac rivers, the Bay of Fundy, the Dorchester and Sackville rivers, and, I believe, in your own constituency, Mr. Speaker. These districts were teeming with shad, which could be bought a few years ago at $3.50 a half barrel. Now, however, it is difficult to get shad at all, the cost being as high as $15 a half barrel. It seems to me that this valuable fishery could be saved to the people of that locality. Some floating shad hatcheries havie been established on the St. John river, but something has been left undone that should have been done to keep up the fisheries along our rivers. I sincerely trust that the ministerhaving heard the remarks of the member for Digby, will get out of -the rut and, with his officers, do something to make our supply of fish as plentiful as it was in the past. If he will promise to take action, we will not vote for the motion of want of confidence, in which case he will be allowed a few weeks to try to do something in the interest of the people.
